category: Define gastritis
coreConcept: Histological definition of Gastropathy vs. Gastritis
front: Gastric mucosal injury is classified as [___] when inflammatory cells are rare or absent, whereas it is termed [___] when neutrophils are histologically present within the mucosa.
back: • Gastropathy: Rare/absent inflammation (caused by NSAIDs, alcohol, or bile). • Gastritis: Presence of neutrophils (indicates active inflammation). • Both may present with epigastric pain and nausea.

category: Define gastritis
front: A 60-year-old female presents with a beefy red tongue, megaloblastic anemia, and achlorhydria. Biopsy reveals diffuse atrophy of the gastric body. Identify the likely diagnosis and the cellular target of the autoantibodies.
back: • Diagnosis: Autoimmune Atrophic Gastritis. • Target: Parietal cells (specifically H+/K+-ATPase) and Intrinsic Factor. • Sequelae: Vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia) and hypergastrinemia.

category: Define gastritis
front: Explain the role of the enzyme urease in the pathogenesis of H. pylori-induced chronic gastritis.
back: • Urease converts urea into ammonia and CO2. • Ammonia elevates local gastric pH (neutralizes acid). • This enhances bacterial survival and colonization within the acidic gastric niche.

category: Define gastritis
front: Contrast H. pylori-associated gastritis with autoimmune gastritis regarding anatomical location and risk of specific malignancies.
back: • H. pylori: Primarily antrum; risk of MALToma and Adenocarcinoma. • Autoimmune: Primarily body/fundus (oxyntic mucosa); risk of Adenocarcinoma and Neuroendocrine (Carcinoid) tumors.

category: Define gastritis
front: State the mechanism by which Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) disrupt gastric mucosal protection.
back: • Inhibition of COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes. • Reduced synthesis of Prostaglandins (E2 and I2). • Decreased bicarbonate/mucus secretion and impaired mucosal blood flow.

category: Define gastritis
front: NSAIDs predispose to gastric injury by inhibiting the cyclooxygenase-dependent synthesis of [___], which are essential for maintaining mucus secretion and mucosal blood flow.
back:
• Prostaglandins (specifically PGE2 and PGI2)
• These mediators also promote bicarbonate secretion and epithelial restitution while reducing gastric acid secretion.

category: Define gastritis
front: A 45-year-old male with severe full-thickness burns over 40% of his body develops multiple shallow gastric ulcers. Identify the specific name and primary mechanism of these lesions.
back:
• Diagnosis: Curling Ulcers
• Mechanism: Systemic hypotension and splanchnic vasoconstriction leading to mucosal ischemia and impaired oxygen delivery.

category: Define gastritis
front: Explain the biological function of the urease enzyme in the survival and pathogenesis of Helicobacter pylori within the stomach.
back:
• Generates ammonia from endogenous urea
• Elevates local gastric pH to protect the bacteria from acidity
• Direct gastric injury via ammonium ion production.

category: Define gastritis
front: Distinguish between the histological inflammatory patterns of H. pylori-associated gastritis and Autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
back:
• H. pylori: Superficial lamina propria infiltrate (neutrophils, plasma cells) in the antrum.
• Autoimmune: Deep inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, macrophages) in the body and fundus, centered on gastric glands.

category: Define gastritis
front: Outline the standard 'Triple Therapy' components used for the eradication of Helicobacter pylori in clinical practice.
back:
• Proton Pump Inhibitor (e.g., Omeprazole)
• Clarithromycin
• Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole if allergic to penicillin).

category: Define gastritis
front: Pathologically, the presence of [___] above the basement membrane in direct contact with epithelial cells is the defining feature that distinguishes gastritis from gastropathy.
back:
• Neutrophils
• This signifies 'active' inflammation; their absence or rarity characterizes gastropathy.

category: Define gastritis
front: A 60-year-old female presents with macrocytic anemia and a 'beefy red' tongue. Gastric biopsy shows atrophy of the body and fundus with intestinal metaplasia. What is the likely underlying pathophysiology?
back:

• Leads to achlorhydria and loss of Intrinsic Factor
• Results in Vitamin B12 deficiency (Pernicious Anemia).

category: Define gastritis
front: How do Cushing ulcers differ from typical stress ulcers in terms of their clinical location and the physiological trigger for acid production?
back:

category: Define gastritis

category: Define gastritis

category: Define gastritis
front: Explain how H. pylori utilizes urease to ensure its survival within the acidic gastric lumen.

category: Define gastritis

back:

category: Define gastritis
front: Identify the primary mechanism by which NSAIDs like Aspirin or Ibuprofen disrupt gastric mucosal protection.

- Decreases mucus/bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow.

category: Define gastritis
front: In autoimmune gastritis, the destruction of parietal cells leads to a deficiency of [___], resulting in Vitamin B12 malabsorption and pernicious anemia.

category: Define gastritis

category: Define gastritis

category: Define gastritis

- Spiral organisms usually visible in overlying mucus.

front: Biopsy of the gastric body in a 60-year-old female with megaloblastic anemia shows diffuse mucosal thinning, loss of parietal cells, and deep lymphocytic infiltrates, while the antrum is spared. Identify the morphology.
back:
- **Autoimmune Atrophic Gastritis**.
- Spares the antrum (oxyntic mucosa focus).
- Deep inflammation (lymphocytes/macrophages) versus superficial H. pylori pattern.
- Frequent intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells).

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Explain the histological composition of the base of a chronic peptic ulcer compared to acute stress-related lesions.
back:
- **Four Classic Layers**: Necrotic debris, active inflammation, granulation tissue, and **fibrotic scarring**.
- Acute stress ulcers characteristically **lack scarring** and blood vessel thickening.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Contrast the microscopic inflammatory profiles of gastropathy versus active gastritis.
back:
- **Gastropathy**: Rare/absent inflammation; foveolar hyperplasia, edema, and vascular congestion predominate.
- **Active Gastritis**: Neutrophils must be present above the basement membrane in contact with epithelial cells.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Describe the lymphoid changes seen in the lamina propria during chronic H. pylori infection and their clinical significance.
back:
- **Induced MALT**: Lymphoid aggregates with germinal centers.
- Subepithelial plasma cell clusters.
- Significant risk factor for transformation into MALT lymphoma.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: The histologic presence of [___] above the basement membrane in direct contact with epithelial cells is the defining feature of active inflammation in gastritis.
back:
• Neutrophils
• Signifies 'active' rather than 'acute' inflammation
• Found among epithelial cells or within mucosal gland lumina.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: A patient with severe burns develops multiple shallow ulcers in the proximal duodenum. Identify the lesion and its primary pathogenesis.
back:
• Curling Ulcers
• Caused by local ischemia
• Due to systemic hypotension and splanchnic vasoconstriction (upregulated endothelin-1).

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Explain how H. pylori survives the acidic gastric environment and its typical microscopic distribution.
back:
• Secretes Urease: Generates ammonia to elevate local pH
• Distribution: Irregular, concentrated in superficial mucus overlying foveolar cells (surface/neck regions).

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Contrast the location and inflammatory depth between H. pylori gastritis and Autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
back:
• H. pylori: Primarily Antrum; superficial lamina propria inflammation
• Autoimmune: Body/Fundus; deep inflammation centered on gastric glands.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Describe the endoscopic and histologic findings characteristic of Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE).
back:
• Endoscopy: Longitudinal stripes of erythematous mucosa (Watermelon Stomach)
• Histology: Dilated mucosal capillaries containing fibrin thrombi.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: In chronic H. pylori infection, the induction of [___] within the lamina propria creates the potential for transformation into MALT lymphoma.
back:
• Lymphoid aggregates (often with germinal centers)
• Represents induced mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT).

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: A 60-year-old female with autoimmune gastritis presents with achlorhydria. What microscopic finding in the gastric body identifies 'intestinal metaplasia'?
back:
• Presence of Goblet cells
• Columnar absorptive cells
• Replacement of foveolar epithelium by intestinal-type mucosa.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Describe the morphology of a 'punched-out' Peptic Ulcer compared to a Malignant Gastric Ulcer.
back:
• Peptic: Round, <1cm, smooth/clean base, margins level with surrounding mucosa
• Malignant: Heaped-up, irregular margins, necrotic base.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Contrast the pathogenic triggers and typical locations of Curling ulcers versus Cushing ulcers.
back:
• Curling: Severe burns/trauma; proximal duodenum
• Cushing: Intracranial disease; stomach, duodenum, or esophagus (vagal stimulation causing hyperacidity).

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Identify the characteristic 'corkscrew' profile often seen in reactive gastropathy or mild acute gastritis.
back:
• Foveolar cell hyperplasia
• Epithelial proliferation
• Accompanied by lamina propria edema and vascular congestion.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: In the gastrointestinal tract, the histological presence of [___] above the basement membrane in direct contact with epithelial cells signifies 'active' gastritis.
back:
Neutrophils.
- Signifies active inflammation.
- Found among epithelial cells or within mucosal gland lumina.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: A 62-year-old female presents with megaloblastic anemia and a beefy red tongue. Gastric biopsy reveals diffuse atrophy of the body and fundus with sparing of the antrum. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
Autoimmune Atrophic Gastritis.
- Characterized by CD4+ T cell-mediated destruction of parietal cells.
- Causes achlorhydria and Vitamin B12 deficiency.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Explain the role of urease in the pathogenesis and morphological colonization of Helicobacter pylori in the stomach.
back:
Urease generates ammonia from urea.
- Elevates local gastric pH.
- Enhances bacterial survival and allows colonization of surface mucus.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Contrast acute stress ulcers with chronic peptic ulcers regarding their usual number, distribution, and the presence of scarring.
back:
Stress Ulcers: Multiple, distributed throughout the stomach, lack fibrotic scarring.
- Peptic Ulcers: Usually solitary, concentrated in the antrum or duodenum, exhibit prominent fibrotic scarring.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Describe the histological appearance of 'pit abscesses' frequently observed in chronic Helicobacter pylori gastritis.
back:
Neutrophils accumulate within the lumens of gastric glands (pits).
- Accompanied by subepithelial plasma cells and lymphoid aggregates in the lamina propria.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: The presence of [___] cells and columnar absorptive cells within the gastric foveolar epithelium defines intestinal metaplasia, a precursor to adenocarcinoma.
back:
Goblet cells.
- Often seen in chronic H. pylori or autoimmune gastritis.
- Represents a response to chronic mucosal injury.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: A patient with cirrhosis presents with hematemesis. Endoscopy shows 'watermelon stomach' (longitudinal erythematous antral stripes). What are the characteristic microscopic findings?
back:
Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE).
- Reactive gastropathy with dilated mucosal capillaries.
- Presence of fibrin thrombi within the capillaries.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: How does the location and inflammatory infiltrate of H. pylori gastritis specifically differ from Autoimmune gastritis?
back:
H. pylori: Primarily antral; neutrophils and subepithelial plasma cells.
- Autoimmune: Body and fundus (oxyntic mucosa); deeper inflammation with lymphocytes and macrophages.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Distinguish 'gastropathy' from 'gastritis' based on the microscopic inflammatory cell profile.
back:
Gastropathy: Inflammatory cells are rare or absent; often caused by NSAIDs, alcohol, or bile.
- Gastritis: Neutrophils are present (active inflammation).

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Identify the potential neoplastic transformation associated with the induced lymphoid aggregates (MALT) seen in chronic H. pylori infection.
back:
B-cell Lymphoma (MALToma).
- Chronic H. pylori triggers lymphoid follicles with germinal centers.
- These can undergo malignant transformation.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Histologically, the term "active inflammation" in the gastric mucosa is specifically defined by the presence of [___] above the basement membrane in direct contact with epithelial cells.
back:
- Neutrophils.
- Indicates active gastritis rather than simple gastropathy.
- May be found in both acute and chronic disease states, reflecting duration rather than pattern.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: A patient with severe burns develops multiple shallow gastric ulcers. These "Curling ulcers" primarily result from which underlying morphological and pathophysiological mechanism?
back:
- Local ischemia.
- Caused by systemic hypotension or splanchnic vasoconstriction.
- Upregulation of endothelin-1 contributes to reduced mucosal blood flow and protective failure.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
coreConcept: H. pylori virulence and survival mechanisms
front: Explain the role of urease and flagella in H. pylori survival and colonization within the gastric environment.
back:
- Urease: Generates ammonia from urea to elevate local pH and survive acidity.
- Flagella: Provide motility, allowing the bacteria to move through viscous mucus toward the epithelium.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
coreConcept: H. pylori vs. Autoimmune Gastritis morphology
front: Contrast H. pylori gastritis and autoimmune atrophic gastritis regarding their primary anatomical location and the depth of inflammatory infiltrate.
back:
- Location: H. pylori focuses on the Antrum; Autoimmune focuses on the Body and Fundus.
- Infiltrate: H. pylori is superficial; Autoimmune is deep and centered on the gastric glands.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Identify the key histological features seen in Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE), also known as watermelon stomach.
back:
- Ectatic mucosal vessels.
- Dilated capillaries containing fibrin thrombi.
- Reactive gastropathy with minimal inflammation and edematous mucosal stripes.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Chronic H. pylori infection often induces the formation of [___] in the gastric mucosa, which are germinal centers that increase the risk of MALT lymphoma.
back:
- Lymphoid aggregates.
- Represent induced mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.
- Found within the superficial lamina propria along with plasma cells and neutrophils.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: An endoscopy of a patient with pernicious anemia reveals diffuse thinning of the gastric body. What morphological hallmark confirms the presence of intestinal metaplasia?
back:
- Presence of Goblet cells.
- Columnar absorptive cells appearing within the gastric foveolar epithelium.
- Associated with a significantly increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Describe the morphological features that distinguish a chronic peptic ulcer from an acute stress-related ulcer.
back:
- Peptic: Solitary, larger (>1cm), located in antrum/duodenum, with significant fibrosis and thickened vessels.
- Stress: Multiple, small (<1cm), anywhere in stomach, lacking fibrotic scarring.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
front: Distinguish the secondary effect of acid secretion on serum gastrin levels in H. pylori antral-predominant gastritis versus autoimmune gastritis.
back:
- H. pylori: Normal to modestly increased gastrin; high acid increases ulcer risk.
- Autoimmune: Markedly increased gastrin (hypergastrinemia) due to achlorhydria-induced G-cell hyperplasia.

category: Describe the morphological features of gastritis
coreConcept: Microscopic zones of a peptic ulcer base
front: List the four distinct histological layers typically found at the base of an active peptic ulcer.
back:
- Fibrinoid/necrotic debris (superficial).
- Nonspecific acute inflammation (neutrophils).
- Granulation tissue.
- Fibrotic/collagenous scar (deepest layer).

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: The cytoprotective molecules inhibited by NSAIDs that normally stimulate mucus secretion, bicarbonate production, and mucosal blood flow are [___].
back:
Prostaglandins (specifically PGE2 and PGI2).
- Maintain mucosal blood flow.
- Stimulate bicarbonate and mucus secretion.
- Promote epithelial restitution.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A patient with a severe intracranial injury develops multiple gastric and esophageal ulcers with a high risk of perforation. Identify the likely pathophysiology.
back:
Cushing Ulcers.
- Caused by direct stimulation of vagal nuclei.
- Results in massive gastric acid hypersecretion.
- Often multiple and sharply demarcated.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Explain the enzymatic mechanism used by Helicobacter pylori to survive the acidic gastric lumen before colonizing the mucus layer.
back:
Urease Production.
- Converts endogenous urea into ammonia.
- Elevates local pH (alkalization).
- Enhances bacterial survival in the acidic environment.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Contrast the typical anatomic location and predominant inflammatory cell type of H. pylori gastritis with autoimmune gastritis.
back:
H. pylori Gastritis:
- Location: Antrum.
- Cells: Neutrophils (active) and subepithelial plasma cells.
Autoimmune Gastritis:
- Location: Body and Fundus.
- Cells: Lymphocytes and macrophages (deep infiltrate).

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Detail the steps by which aspirin ingestion leads to acute erosive hemorrhagic gastritis beyond simple direct chemical irritation.
back:
COX-1/COX-2 Inhibition.
- Blocks prostaglandin synthesis.
- Reduces bicarbonate/mucus defense.
- Decreases mucosal blood flow, leading to ischemic-like injury.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: The histological presence of [___] in the lamina propria during chronic H. pylori infection indicates the potential for transformation into MALT lymphoma.
back:
Lymphoid Aggregates.
- Often contain germinal centers.
- Represent induced mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.
- Risk factor for B-cell lymphoma.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A 60-year-old female with Graves disease presents with megaloblastic anemia and achlorhydria. Link the stomach findings to the hematological presentation.
back:
Autoimmune Atrophic Gastritis.
- CD4+ T-cells destroy Parietal cells.
- Loss of Intrinsic Factor.
- Failure of Vitamin B12 absorption leads to Pernicious Anemia.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Distinguish between the microscopic definitions of 'active gastritis' and 'gastropathy' based on inflammatory cell presence.
back:
Active Gastritis:
- Neutrophils present above the basement membrane (intraepithelial).
Gastropathy:
- Cell injury/regeneration present.
- Inflammatory cells are rare or absent.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Describe the physiological loop leading to hypergastrinemia in patients with autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
back:
Parietal Cell Loss.
- Leads to achlorhydria (low acid).
- Lack of negative feedback on G-cells.
- Results in G-cell hyperplasia and massive gastrin release.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Identify the pathognomonic microscopic marker of 'intestinal metaplasia' found in chronic gastritis that increases adenocarcinoma risk.
back:
Presence of Goblet Cells.
- Replacement of foveolar epithelium with intestinal-type cells.
- Associated with chronic H. pylori or autoimmune injury.
- Precursor to dysplasia.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: NSAIDs cause gastric mucosal injury primarily by inhibiting the enzyme [___], thereby reducing the synthesis of protective prostaglandins E2 and I2.
back:
* Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2)
* Reduces mucus and bicarbonate secretion
* Impairs mucosal blood flow and epithelial restitution.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A patient with severe head trauma develops multiple shallow gastric ulcers. Identify the specific name for these ulcers and the underlying physiological mechanism.
back:
* Cushing Ulcers
* Mechanism: Increased intracranial pressure stimulates vagal nuclei
* Results in gastric acid hypersecretion.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Explain how H. pylori survives the highly acidic environment of the gastric lumen to establish chronic infection.
back:
* Secretes Urease enzyme
* Converts urea into ammonia and CO2
* Creates a protective local alkaline 'cloud' (pH elevation) around the bacteria.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
coreConcept: Autoimmune Atrophic Gastritis vs H. Pylori Gastritis
front: A 60-year-old female presents with megaloblastic anemia and achlorhydria. Contrast the histological location and specific cell loss in this condition versus typical H. pylori gastritis.
back:
* Location: Body/Fundus (Autoimmune) vs. Antrum (H. pylori)
* Cell Loss: Parietal and Chief cells (Autoimmune) vs. Superficial foveolar damage
* Infiltrate: Deep/Gland-centered (Autoimmune) vs. Superficial.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Identify the specific histological finding that distinguishes 'active' gastritis from simple gastropathy in a biopsy specimen.
back:
* Presence of neutrophils
* Neutrophils must be above the basement membrane
* Often found within epithelial layers or gland lumina (pit abscesses).

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: The formation of [___] with germinal centers in the gastric lamina propria during chronic H. pylori infection is a high-yield diagnostic marker for MALToma risk.
back:
* Lymphoid aggregates
* Represents induced mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue
* Carries potential for transformation into B-cell lymphoma.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A burn victim hospitalized for 48 hours develops coffee-ground emesis. Identify the likely lesion and its primary pathogenic driver.
back:
* Curling Ulcer (Proximal duodenum)
* Driver: Systemic hypotension and hypovolemia
* Leads to mucosal ischemia and impaired oxygen delivery.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Detail the mechanism by which autoimmune atrophic gastritis results in subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.
back:
* Autoimmune destruction of Parietal cells
* Loss of Intrinsic Factor secretion
* Defective Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum
* Resultant megaloblastic anemia and demyelination.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Distinguish the microscopic appearance of 'intestinal metaplasia' from normal gastric mucosa in the setting of chronic injury.
back:
* Presence of Goblet cells (absent in normal stomach)
* Appearance of columnar absorptive cells
* Significant risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma development.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: List three common chemical or physiological irritants that typically cause 'gastropathy' (injury without inflammation) rather than true gastritis.
back:
* Chronic NSAID use
* Excessive alcohol consumption
* Bile reflux
* Uremic toxins.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: In the pathogenesis of acute gastropathy, NSAIDs induce mucosal injury primarily by inhibiting the synthesis of [___], which are essential for mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
back: Prostaglandins (E2 and I2). They maintain mucosal blood flow and epithelial restitution. Inhibition of COX-1 and COX-2 disrupts these protective mechanisms.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A patient in the ICU with severe burns develops multiple shallow gastric and duodenal ulcers. Identify the specific name for these ulcers and the primary underlying mechanism.
back: Curling ulcers. Caused by mucosal ischemia due to systemic hypotension or splanchnic vasoconstriction (mediated by endothelin-1) during severe physiologic stress.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: How does H. pylori survive the highly acidic environment of the gastric lumen to establish chronic infection?
back: Urease secretion converts urea into ammonia and CO2, neutralizing local acid. Flagella provide motility through viscous mucus to reach neutral-pH foveolar cells.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Contrast the anatomical location and inflammatory infiltrate of H. pylori-associated gastritis versus Autoimmune gastritis.
back: H. pylori: Primarily Antrum; neutrophils, plasma cells, and lymphoid aggregates. Autoimmune: Body and Fundus (antrum spared); deep lymphocytic and macrophage infiltrate with parietal cell loss.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Identify the relationship between chronic H. pylori infection and the formation of Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT).
back: Chronic inflammation induces organized lymphoid aggregates in the gastric wall. These B-cell clusters can undergo malignant transformation into MALT lymphoma.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: In the gastrointestinal tract, the presence of [___] above the basement membrane in direct contact with epithelial cells is the hallmark of active gastritis.
back: Neutrophils. Their presence signifies 'active' inflammation regardless of disease duration. They may accumulate in gland lumens to form 'pit abscesses'.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A 60-year-old female presents with a beefy red tongue, megaloblastic anemia, and achlorhydria. Gastric biopsy shows atrophy of the body and fundus. What is the target of the autoantibodies?
back: Parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase and Intrinsic Factor. This leads to Vitamin B12 deficiency (Pernicious Anemia) and hypergastrinemia due to lack of acid feedback.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Describe the specific mechanism causing Cushing ulcers in patients with intracranial trauma.
back: Direct stimulation of vagal nuclei leads to gastric acid hypersecretion. Unlike typical stress ulcers, Cushing ulcers have a high risk of perforation.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Distinguish the acid production and gastrin levels between H. pylori antral-predominant gastritis and autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
back: H. pylori (Antral): Increased acid and slightly increased gastrin. Autoimmune: Decreased acid (achlorhydria) and markedly increased gastrin (hypergastrinemia).

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Define the morphologic feature 'intestinal metaplasia' in chronic gastritis and state its clinical significance.
back: Presence of goblet cells and columnar absorptive cells in gastric mucosa. It is a precursor lesion for gastric adenocarcinoma, especially in autoimmune gastritis.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: NSAIDs induce gastric injury primarily by inhibiting the enzyme [___], which reduces the synthesis of cytoprotective prostaglandins E2 and I2.
back:
Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2).
- Prostaglandins stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
- They enhance mucosal blood flow and epithelial restitution.
- Inhibition leads to impaired mucosal defense.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A 45-year-old male with a severe traumatic brain injury develops multiple gastric ulcers. Identify the specific name and mechanism for these lesions.
back:
Cushing Ulcers.
- Caused by direct stimulation of vagal nuclei.
- Results in gastric acid hypersecretion.
- Higher risk of perforation compared to standard stress ulcers.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Explain how the bacterial enzyme urease facilitates the survival of Helicobacter pylori in the acidic gastric environment.
back:
Converts endogenous urea into ammonia and CO2.
- Ammonia buffers gastric acid, elevating local pH.
- Creates a neutral microenvironment around the bacteria.
- Essential for bacterial survival and colonization in mucus.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Contrast H. pylori-associated gastritis and autoimmune atrophic gastritis regarding primary anatomical location and acid production status.
back:
H. pylori: Predominantly Antrum; acid is normal or increased.
- Autoimmune: Body and Fundus; results in achlorhydria (low acid).
- H. pylori leads to peptic ulcers; Autoimmune leads to pernicious anemia.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Identify the long-term neoplastic complication associated with the lymphoid aggregates and germinal centers induced by chronic H. pylori infection.
back:
MALToma (Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue lymphoma).
- Chronic B-cell proliferation leads to malignant transformation.
- May regress after successful H. pylori eradication.
- Associated with increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: In the context of the GI tract, the presence of [___] above the basement membrane in direct contact with epithelial cells signifies active inflammation.
back:
Neutrophils.
- Termed 'active' regardless of overall chronicity.
- Accumulate in gland lumens to form 'pit abscesses'.
- Distinguishes gastritis from simple gastropathy.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A patient with chronic body-predominant gastritis presents with megaloblastic anemia and a beefy red tongue. Specify the physiological deficiency causing these findings.
back:
Vitamin B12 deficiency.
- CD4+ T-cells destroy parietal cells.
- Loss of Intrinsic Factor prevents ileal B12 absorption.
- Termed Pernicious Anemia; associated with autoimmune atrophic gastritis.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Distinguish the gross morphological appearance and distribution of acute stress-related ulcers from chronic peptic ulcers.
back:
Stress Ulcers: Multiple, shallow, <1cm, found anywhere in stomach.
- Peptic Ulcers: Usually solitary, punched-out, antrum or duodenum.
- Peptic ulcers show base fibrosis/scarring; stress ulcers lack scarring.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Compare the levels of serum gastrin in H. pylori-associated antral gastritis versus autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
back:
Autoimmune: Marked hypergastrinemia (due to achlorhydria).
- H. pylori: Normal or modestly increased gastrin.
- Autoimmune achlorhydria removes negative feedback, causing antral G-cell hyperplasia.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Specify the eponym for proximal duodenal ulcers occurring specifically in the setting of severe burns or trauma.
back:
Curling Ulcers.
- Located in the proximal duodenum.
- Result of systemic hypotension and reduced mucosal blood flow.
- Ischemic injury is the primary pathogenic mechanism.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: NSAIDs cause gastric mucosal injury primarily by inhibiting the enzyme [___], thereby reducing the synthesis of protective prostaglandins E2 and I2.
back:
- Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2).
- Prostaglandins stimulate mucus/bicarbonate secretion and maintain mucosal blood flow.
- Deficiency leads to impaired epithelial restitution and increased acid susceptibility.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A patient with a severe traumatic brain injury develops multiple acute gastric ulcers with a high risk of perforation. Identify the specific ulcer type and its underlying pathophysiology.
back:
- Diagnosis: Cushing Ulcers.
- Pathophysiology: Direct stimulation of vagal nuclei by intracranial pressure.
- Result: Excessive gastric acid hypersecretion leading to mucosal erosion.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Explain how Helicobacter pylori utilizes the enzyme urease to survive in the highly acidic environment of the stomach.
back:
- Urease converts endogenous urea into ammonia and CO2.
- Ammonia elevates local gastric pH.
- This creates a neutral microenvironment ('cloud') for bacterial survival and colonization.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Contrast H. pylori-associated gastritis and autoimmune atrophic gastritis regarding their primary anatomical location and specific serum antibody findings.
back:
- H. pylori: Predominantly Antrum; Antibodies against H. pylori organisms.
- Autoimmune: Body and Fundus (Oxyntic mucosa); Antibodies against Parietal cells (H+/K+-ATPase) and Intrinsic Factor.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Outline the standard components of the first-line 'Triple Therapy' for the eradication of Helicobacter pylori.
back:
- Proton Pump Inhibitor (e.g., Omeprazole).
- Clarithromycin.
- Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole for penicillin-allergic patients).

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: In the setting of severe burns or trauma, stress-related ulcers that typically occur in the proximal duodenum are known as [___] ulcers.
back:
- Curling Ulcers.
- Caused by systemic hypotension and reduced mucosal blood flow (ischemia).
- Usually present as shallow, multiple erosions.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A 60-year-old female with chronic body-predominant gastritis presents with a 'beefy red' tongue and macrocytic anemia. Explain the link between her gastric pathology and her hematological findings.
back:
- Autoimmune destruction of Parietal cells causes loss of Intrinsic Factor.
- Intrinsic Factor is required for Vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum.
- Result: Pernicious anemia (megaloblastic) due to B12 deficiency.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Describe the histological finding in chronic H. pylori gastritis that increases the risk of B-cell lymphoma (MALToma).
back:
- Induced Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT).
- Visible as lymphoid aggregates with germinal centers in the lamina propria.
- Chronic antigenic stimulation promotes B-cell transformation.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Distinguish between the terms 'gastritis' and 'gastropathy' based on the presence of inflammatory cells.
back:
- Gastritis: Inflammatory cells (neutrophils) are present above the basement membrane.
- Gastropathy: Epithelial injury and regeneration are present, but inflammatory cells are rare or absent.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Identify the high-yield virulence factor of H. pylori strongly linked to the development of gastric adenocarcinoma and intestinal metaplasia.
back:
- Cytotoxin-associated gene A (CagA).
- Present in approximately 90% of isolates in high-risk populations.
- Induces proinflammatory cytokine secretion and epithelial atrophy.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Gastric mucosal injury from NSAIDs is primarily mediated by the inhibition of [___], which reduces the synthesis of protective prostaglandins E2 and I2.
back:
• Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2)
• Results in decreased mucus and bicarbonate secretion
• Reduces mucosal blood flow and epithelial restitution

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A 45-year-old male with severe body surface area burns develops multiple shallow gastric erosions and hematemesis. These specific stress-induced lesions are known as [___].
back:
• Curling Ulcers
• Pathogenesis: Systemic hypotension and splanchnic vasoconstriction leading to mucosal ischemia
• Usually located in the proximal duodenum or stomach

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Explain the role of the enzyme Urease in ensuring the survival of Helicobacter pylori within the hostile acidic environment of the stomach.
back:
• Converts urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide
• Generates a local alkaline 'cloud' to neutralize gastric acid
• Ammonium ions directly damage the gastric mucosal barrier

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A patient with megaloblastic anemia and glossitis has atrophy of the gastric body but a normal antrum. Contrast this condition's pathophysiology with common H. pylori-associated gastritis.
back:
• Autoimmune (Body): CD4+ T-cell destruction of parietal cells; causes achlorhydria and hypergastrinemia
• H. pylori (Antrum): Bacterial virulence (urease/toxins); produces lymphoid aggregates and increases peptic ulcer risk

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Identify the specific inflammatory cell whose presence above the basement membrane within the epithelium signifies 'active' gastritis.
back:
• Neutrophils (intraepithelial)
• Indicates active inflammation regardless of disease duration
• Often associated with 'pit abscesses' in the gastric glands

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: In the pathogenesis of NSAID-induced gastritis, the inhibition of [___] leads to decreased synthesis of protective prostaglandins E2 and I2.
back:
Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2).
* Prostaglandins stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
* They maintain mucosal blood flow.
* Inhibition impairs epithelial restitution and defenses.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A 45-year-old male with a severe traumatic brain injury develops multiple acute gastric ulcers. Identify this specific ulcer type and its primary physiological trigger.
back:
Cushing ulcer; Vagal nuclei stimulation.
* Intracranial pressure stimulates vagus nerve.
* Leads to gastric acid hypersecretion.
* High risk of perforation compared to other stress ulcers.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Explain the role of H. pylori-derived urease in facilitating bacterial survival within the acidic gastric lumen.
back:
Urease converts urea into ammonia and CO2.
* Ammonia buffers gastric acid, elevating local pH.
* Creates a neutral microenvironment for colonization.
* Forms the basis of the Urea Breath Test.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A patient presents with megaloblastic anemia and achlorhydria. Contrast the typical gastric biopsy site and inflammatory pattern of this condition with H. pylori gastritis.
back:
Autoimmune Gastritis: Body/Fundus; diffuse atrophy; deep inflammation.
* H. pylori Gastritis: Antrum; patchy involvement; superficial plasma cells.
* Autoimmune spares the antrum and involves parietal cell antibodies.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Identify the three essential components of the 'Triple Therapy' regimen used for the eradication of H. pylori chronic gastritis.
back:
Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) + Two Antibiotics.
* Antibiotics: Usually Clarithromycin and Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole).
* PPI increases pH to enhance antibiotic activity.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Histologically, the presence of [___] above the basement membrane in direct contact with epithelial cells is the hallmark of active gastritis.
back:
Neutrophils.
* Signifies 'active' inflammation regardless of disease duration.
* Distinguishes gastritis from gastropathy (where inflammation is minimal).
* May form pit abscesses within gastric glands.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A 60-year-old female presents with a beefy red tongue and loss of vibration sense. Biopsy shows intestinal metaplasia in the gastric body. Explain the mechanism of her anemia.
back:
Vitamin B12 deficiency (Pernicious Anemia).
* Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells.
* Leads to loss of Intrinsic Factor secretion.
* Results in defective B12 absorption in the ileum.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Why is chronic H. pylori infection of the gastric body associated with an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma compared to antral-limited infection?
back:
Body involvement leads to multifocal atrophic gastritis.
* Associated with CagA+ strains and proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1̢).
* Leads to parietal cell loss and intestinal metaplasia.
* Metaplasia acts as a precursor for dysplasia/carcinoma.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Contrast the serum gastrin levels found in H. pylori antral-predominant gastritis with those found in autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
back:
H. pylori: Normal to modestly increased gastrin.
* Autoimmune: Markedly increased (Hypergastrinemia).
* In autoimmune, achlorhydria removes negative feedback on G-cells.
* High gastrin causes neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Identify the primary clinical association and typical anatomical location of Curling ulcers.
back:
Severe burns or major trauma.
* Located in the proximal duodenum.
* Caused by mucosal ischemia due to splanchnic vasoconstriction.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: The bacterial enzyme [___] allows H. pylori to survive the acidic gastric environment by generating ammonia from endogenous urea.
back:
• Urease
• Raises local gastric pH
• Enhances bacterial survival and colonization in the mucus layer.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A patient with severe intracranial trauma develops acute gastric ulcers with a high risk of perforation. Identify this specific ulcer type and its primary cause.
back:
• Cushing Ulcers
• Caused by direct stimulation of vagal nuclei
• Leads to hypersecretion of gastric acid.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Explain the role of Prostaglandins E2 and I2 in maintaining the gastric mucosal barrier.
back:
• Stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion
• Promote mucosal blood flow
• Enhance epithelial regenerative capacity and reduce acid secretion.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A 45-year-old male describes epigastric burning that occurs 2 hours after meals and is relieved by eating. Contrast this with the pain pattern typically seen in gastric ulcers.
back:
• Duodenal Ulcer: Pain 1–3 hours post-meals, relieved by food/alkali, worse at night.
• Gastric Ulcer: Pain occurs sooner after eating; food may aggravate symptoms.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Identify the standard pharmacological components of 'Triple Therapy' used for H. pylori eradication.
back:
• Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI)
• Clarithromycin
• Amoxicillin or Metronidazole.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Histologically, the base of a chronic peptic ulcer consists of four layers: necrotic debris, nonspecific acute inflammation, [___], and [___].
back:
• Granulation tissue
• Fibrotic scarring (S)
• Scarring is absent in acute stress ulcers.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A patient presents with sudden, severe abdominal pain and 'free air under the diaphragm' on an upright radiograph. Identify the most likely underlying complication of PUD.
back:
• Acute Perforation
• Occurs in up to 5% of patients
• Accounts for two-thirds of ulcer-related deaths.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Describe the pathogenesis of peptic ulcers in Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome.
back:
• Gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma)
• Massive hypergastrinemia stimulates parietal cells
• Causes extreme gastric acid hypersecretion and multiple refractory ulcers.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Contrast the typical number and location of acute stress ulcers versus chronic peptic ulcers.
back:
• Stress Ulcers: Usually multiple; found anywhere in the stomach.
• Peptic Ulcers: Usually solitary; found in proximal duodenum or gastric antrum.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Which specific anatomical site is the most frequent location for the development of Peptic Ulcer Disease?
back:
• Proximal duodenum
• Usually within a few centimeters of the pyloric valve
• Associated with H. pylori-induced antral gastritis.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Peptic ulcers associated with chronic NSAID use result primarily from the inhibition of [___], which leads to a decrease in protective prostaglandins E2 and I2.
back:
• Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2)
• Prostaglandins normally enhance mucus/bicarbonate secretion.
• Loss reduces mucosal blood flow and impairs epithelial regenerative capacity.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A patient with a severe intracranial injury develops multiple gastric and duodenal ulcers. Identify the specific name for these lesions and the primary neurogenic mechanism involved.
back:
• Cushing ulcers
• Caused by direct stimulation of vagal nuclei.
• Vagal hyperactivity leads to excessive gastric acid secretion (hyperacidity).

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Explain how the bacterial enzyme urease facilitates the survival of H. pylori within the acidic gastric environment.
back:
• Urease converts endogenous urea into ammonia and CO2.
• Ammonia neutralizes local gastric acid.
• Creates an alkaline 'cloud' that protects the bacteria from low pH.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A 45-year-old male presents with a solitary, sharply 'punched-out' mucosal defect with smooth margins. Contrast this with the typical margins seen in a malignant gastric ulcer.
back:
• Benign Peptic Ulcer: Sharp, 'punched-out' margins level with the mucosa.
• Malignant Ulcer: Heaped-up, irregular, or beaded margins.
• Benign ulcers usually lack significant surrounding mucosal thickening.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: List the four histological layers found in the base of a chronic, active peptic ulcer, starting from the luminal surface.
back:
• 1. Necrotic debris and fibrinoid exudate.
• 2. Nonspecific acute inflammation (neutrophilic).
• 3. Vascularized granulation tissue.
• 4. Fibrotic, collagenous scar.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: In H. pylori-associated gastritis, the organisms are most concentrated within the [___] overlying the epithelial cells of the antrum.
back:
• Superficial mucus layer
• Bacteria use flagella for motility within the viscous mucus.
• They preferentially colonize the antrum rather than the oxyntic mucosa.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A 30-year-old female reports epigastric burning that is relieved by eating but recurs 2 hours later. Identify the most likely anatomical site of the ulcer.
back:
• Proximal Duodenum
• Usually within a few centimeters of the pyloric valve.
• Pain occurs when acid enters the duodenum without food buffering.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Why does H. pylori infection limited to the antrum typically result in duodenal ulcers rather than gastric atrophy?
back:
• Antral inflammation increases gastrin production.
• Elevated gastrin stimulates parietal cell mass in the body.
• Results in hyperacidity, which damages the duodenal mucosa.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Distinguish acute stress-related ulcers from chronic peptic ulcers based on their typical number and presence of scarring.
back:
• Stress Ulcers: Multiple, shallow, lacking deep fibrotic scarring.
• Chronic Peptic Ulcers: Usually solitary, deep, with a thick fibrotic base.
• Healing of stress ulcers usually leaves no permanent scar.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Identify the most frequent clinical complication of peptic ulcer disease that may present as melena or hematemesis.
back:
• Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage (Bleeding)
• Occurs in 15% to 20% of patients.
• Caused by erosion into an underlying artery in the ulcer base.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: In the pathogenesis of peptic ulcer disease, the enzyme [___] produced by H. pylori neutralizes gastric acid by generating ammonia, thereby facilitating bacterial survival in the acidic lumen.
back:
* Urease
* Converts urea into ammonia and CO2
* Creates a neutral microenvironment for the bacteria
* Essential for initial colonization of the gastric mucosa

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A 70-year-old patient on long-term therapy for osteoarthritis presents with epigastric pain and melena. Endoscopy reveals a solitary antral ulcer. Explain the biochemical mechanism of injury in this patient.
back:
* NSAID-induced COX-1 and COX-2 inhibition
* Depletion of protective prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2)
* Reduced bicarbonate and mucus secretion
* Decreased mucosal blood flow and impaired epithelial repair

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: How does the 'unstirred layer' of mucus protect the gastric epithelium from autodigestion?
back:
* Physical barrier against food and pepsin
* Traps secreted bicarbonate ions
* Maintains a neutral pH at the cell surface
* Prevents back-diffusion of hydrogen ions into the lamina propria

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Contrast the gross morphological features of a classic chronic peptic ulcer with those of a gastric adenocarcinoma.
back:
* Peptic: Small (<3cm), sharply "punched-out," margins level with surrounding mucosa
* Malignant: Large, irregular, "heaped-up" or beaded margins
* Base: Peptic base is clean/smooth; Malignant base is necrotic/irregular

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Characterize the difference between Curling and Cushing ulcers regarding their clinical etiology and primary location.
back:
* Curling: Associated with severe burns/trauma; located in proximal duodenum
* Cushing: Associated with intracranial disease/surgery; located in stomach, duodenum, or esophagus
* Cushing ulcers carry a higher risk of perforation

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: The base of a chronic peptic ulcer classically consists of four histological zones, starting from the surface: necrotic debris, nonspecific acute inflammation, [___], and finally, a fibrotic scar.
back:
* Granulation tissue
* Rich in immature vessels and mononuclear leukocytes
* Provides the vascular framework for healing
* Distinguishes chronic ulcers from acute erosions

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A patient with a history of recurrent epigastric pain suddenly develops 'board-like' abdominal rigidity. An upright X-ray shows air under the diaphragm. What is the most likely morphological complication?
back:
* Perforation into the peritoneal cavity
* Leads to chemical then bacterial peritonitis
* Usually involves the anterior duodenal wall or gastric antrum
* A surgical emergency secondary to transmural ulceration

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Explain how H. pylori infection localized strictly to the gastric antrum leads to duodenal ulcer formation.
back:
* Antral inflammation decreases somatostatin-producing D cells
* Leads to disinhibition of gastrin release (hypergastrinemia)
* Increased gastrin stimulates parietal cell mass and acid secretion
* High acid load overwhelms duodenal mucosal defenses

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Distinguish acute stress-related mucosal disease from chronic peptic ulcer disease based on number and location.
back:
* Stress ulcers: Typically multiple, small (<1cm), and found anywhere in the stomach
* Chronic PUD: Usually solitary, larger, and localized to the antrum or proximal duodenum
* Stress ulcers lack the extensive scarring seen in PUD

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Identify the most common anatomical site for the development of a peptic ulcer.
back:
* Proximal duodenum
* Usually within a few centimeters of the pyloric valve
* Often involves the anterior or posterior wall
* Linked to high acid output from the stomach

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: The bacterial enzyme [___] allows H. pylori to survive the acidic gastric environment by converting urea into ammonia, thereby raising the local pH.
back: • Urease. • Neutralizes gastric acid locally. • Essential for bacterial colonization within the gastric mucus layer.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A 45-year-old male presents with chronic epigastric pain that is relieved by food and antacids. Endoscopy reveals a solitary, sharply demarcated defect in the proximal duodenum. Identify the most likely underlying infection.
back: • Helicobacter pylori. • Most common cause of duodenal ulcers. • Leads to antral-predominant gastritis and gastric hyperacidity.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Explain how the chronic use of Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) leads to the development of gastric ulcers.
back: • Inhibition of COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes. • Reduces synthesis of mucosal Prostaglandins (E2 and I2). • Impairs mucus secretion, bicarbonate production, and mucosal blood flow.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Contrast the gross morphological margins of a benign peptic ulcer with those of a malignant gastric adenocarcinoma.
back: • Benign: Sharply punched-out, smooth, level margins. • Malignant: Heaped-up, irregular, or beaded margins. • Peptic ulcers lack significant surrounding mucosal thickening.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: List the four characteristic histological layers found in the base of a chronic active peptic ulcer from superficial to deep.
back: • Necrotic debris (fibrinoid). • Nonspecific acute inflammation (neutrophils). • Granulation tissue. • Fibrosis/collagenous scar.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Peptic ulcers located along the [___] curvature of the stomach near the interface of the body and antrum are most characteristic of chronic H. pylori infection.
back: • Lesser curvature. • Most common site for gastric peptic ulcers. • Often associated with chronic antral-predominant inflammation.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A patient with a known history of peptic ulcer disease presents with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain and "free air under the diaphragm" on an upright X-ray. Specify the most likely complication.
back: • Perforation. • A surgical emergency involving the peritoneal cavity. • Significant cause of ulcer-related mortality.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: How does cigarette smoking synergize with other risk factors to increase the severity and recurrence of peptic ulcer disease?
back: • Reduces mucosal blood flow and oxygenation. • Impairs angiogenesis and mucosal healing. • Increases the risk of duodenal and gastric ulceration.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Distinguish between the pain patterns of gastric ulcers and duodenal ulcers in relation to food intake.
back: • Gastric: Pain often worsens shortly after eating. • Duodenal: Pain occurs 1-3 hours post-meals and is relieved by food/alkali. • Night pain is more common in duodenal ulcers.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Name the specific H. pylori virulence factor protein strongly associated with an increased risk of progressing to gastric adenocarcinoma and intestinal metaplasia.
back: • Cytotoxin-associated gene A (CagA). • Associated with more virulent bacterial strains. • Promotes proinflammatory cytokine secretion and epithelial damage.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Gastric mucosal protection is primarily maintained by [___], which promote bicarbonate secretion, mucus production, and adequate mucosal blood flow.
back:
Prostaglandins (specifically PGE2 and PGI2).
- Stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
- Maintain mucosal blood flow.
- Facilitate epithelial regenerative capacity.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A 45-year-old male with chronic epigastric pain tests positive on a urea breath test. Describe the mechanism by which the causal organism survives the acidic gastric environment.
back:
Helicobacter pylori produces urease:
- Converts endogenous urea into ammonia and CO2.
- Ammonia neutralizes local gastric acid.
- Creates a neutral pH micro-environment for bacterial survival.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which chronic use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) leads to peptic ulceration.
back:
Systemic inhibition of COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes:
- Blocks prostaglandin synthesis.
- Reduces bicarbonate and mucus 'unstirred layer' thickness.
- Decreases mucosal blood flow and impairs epithelial repair.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Contrast the gross morphological margins of a benign chronic peptic ulcer with those of a malignant gastric ulcer.
back:
Benign Ulcer:
- Punched-out, sharp margins level with surrounding mucosa.
- Smooth base with radiating mucosal folds.
Malignant Ulcer:
- Heaped-up, irregular, or beaded margins.
- Necrotic, irregular base.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: List the components of the standard 'Triple Therapy' used for the eradication of Helicobacter pylori in Pakistani clinical practice.
back:
- Proton Pump Inhibitor (e.g., Omeprazole).
- Clarithromycin.
- Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole for penicillin-allergic patients).
- Duration is typically 10 to 14 days.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Stress-induced ulcers occurring specifically in the proximal duodenum following severe burns or major trauma are known as [___] ulcers.
back:
Curling ulcers.
- Caused by systemic hypotension and mucosal ischemia.
- Found in the proximal duodenum.
- Contrast with Cushing ulcers (intracranial-related).

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A patient with a history of untreated peptic ulcer disease presents with sudden-onset board-like abdominal rigidity. Upright X-ray shows air under the diaphragm. Identify the likely complication.
back:
Acute Perforation:
- Surgical emergency leading to chemical peritonitis.
- Pneumoperitoneum (free air) is pathognomonic.
- Most common in anterior duodenal ulcers.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Describe the unique pathogenesis of Cushing ulcers associated with intracranial injury.
back:
Direct stimulation of vagal nuclei:
- Leads to hypersecretion of gastric acid via acetylcholine.
- High risk of perforation.
- Can involve the stomach, duodenum, or esophagus.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Distinguish between the acid secretion patterns in H. pylori antral-predominant gastritis versus H. pylori pangastritis.
back:
Antral-predominant:
- Hypergastrinemia and high acid production; high duodenal ulcer risk.
Pangastritis:
- Widespread mucosal atrophy, low acid production; high gastric adenocarcinoma risk.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Identify the four classic histological layers found in the base of an active chronic peptic ulcer, ordered from the lumen downward.
back:
1. Fibrinoid necrotic debris.
2. Zone of active inflammation (neutrophils).
3. Granulation tissue.
4. Fibrous/collagenous scar (forming the ulcer base).

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: In the pathogenesis of NSAID-induced gastropathy, the primary mechanism of injury is the systemic inhibition of [___], which impairs mucosal protection by reducing prostaglandin E2 and I2 levels.
back: • Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) enzymes. • Leads to decreased mucus and bicarbonate secretion. • Reduces mucosal blood flow and epithelial regenerative capacity.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A 25-year-old male with 40% total body surface area burns develops multiple shallow ulcers in the proximal duodenum. Identify these specific stress-related lesions.
back: • Curling ulcers. • Pathogenesis involves systemic hypotension and stress-induced splanchnic vasoconstriction. • Leads to reduced oxygen delivery and local mucosal ischemia.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Explain how the Helicobacter pylori urease enzyme facilitates the biochemical mechanism used for its survival and clinical diagnosis.
back: • Urease converts endogenous urea into ammonia and CO2. • Ammonia neutralizes gastric acid to create a protective alkaline microenvironment. • This mechanism is the basis for the Urea Breath Test.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Contrast the clinical association and typical anatomical location of Curling ulcers with those of Cushing ulcers.
back: • Curling: Associated with severe burns or trauma; located in the proximal duodenum. • Cushing: Associated with intracranial disease; located in the stomach, duodenum, or esophagus. • Cushing ulcers have higher perforation risk.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Explain why prostaglandin analogs or proton pump inhibitors are necessary for patients on long-term non-selective NSAID therapy.
back: • NSAIDs deplete protective prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2). • Depletion impairs the physical mucus barrier and bicarbonate secretion. • These drugs restore mucosal defenses or eliminate the acid challenge to prevent erosions.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: On histological examination of H. pylori-infected antral mucosa, the presence of [___] is a characteristic finding that represents induced MALT and carries a risk of transformation into lymphoma.
back: • Lymphoid aggregates with germinal centers. • Located in the superficial lamina propria. • Chronic stimulation can lead to B-cell MALT lymphoma (MALToma).

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: A 60-year-old female presents with atrophic glossitis and paresthesias. Gastric biopsy shows diffuse atrophy of the body and fundus with antral sparing. Identify the diagnosis and the specific immune target.
back: • Autoimmune atrophic gastritis. • CD4+ T-cells and antibodies target Parietal cells (H+⁄K+ ATPase) and Intrinsic Factor. • Results in achlorhydria and Vitamin B12 deficiency (Pernicious anemia).

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Explain the mechanism by which antral-predominant H. pylori infection increases the risk of duodenal ulcers compared to pangastritis.
back: • Antral inflammation reduces local somatostatin levels. • This causes hypergastrinemia and increased parietal cell mass. • Resultant hyperacidity leads to peptic ulceration in the duodenum.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Contrast the histological definitions of 'gastropathy' and 'active gastritis' based on the inflammatory cell profile.
back: • Gastropathy: Inflammatory cells are rare or absent; caused by irritants (alcohol, bile, NSAIDs). • Active Gastritis: Neutrophils are present within the epithelium or gland lumina. • Chronic Gastritis features lymphocytes and plasma cells.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
front: Describe the endoscopic appearance and clinical association of Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE).
back: • Longitudinal stripes of edematous, erythematous mucosa ('Watermelon Stomach'). • Erythema is created by ectatic mucosal vessels with fibrin thrombi. • Often associated with cirrhosis and systemic sclerosis.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: The bacterial enzyme [___] produced by H. pylori converts urea into ammonia to neutralize gastric acid and facilitate mucosal colonization.
back:
Urease. Key points:
- Raises local pH to ensure bacterial survival.
- Generates ammonia, which is directly toxic to gastric epithelial cells.
- Facilitates bacterial motility through mucus.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A 65-year-old patient on long-term ibuprofen for osteoarthritis presents with new-onset epigastric pain. Explain the primary biochemical defect causing this injury.
back:
Cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibition. Key points:
- Decreases synthesis of protective prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2).
- Reduces mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
- Impairs mucosal blood flow and epithelial regeneration.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Describe the pathogenetic role of the H. pylori cytotoxin-associated gene A (CagA) in gastric mucosal injury.
back:
Pathogenesis mechanism:
- Injected into host cells via a type IV secretion system.
- Induces proinflammatory cytokine release (e.g., IL-8).
- Promotes epithelial proliferation and increases the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A patient with a chronic duodenal ulcer presents with sudden, severe abdominal pain and 'free air' under the diaphragm on X-ray. Identify the complication and its typical anatomical site.
back:
Perforation. Key points:
- Most common in ulcers on the anterior wall of the duodenum.
- Results in leakage of luminal contents into the peritoneal cavity.
- Identified as a surgical emergency.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Summarize the four classic histological layers found at the base of an active chronic peptic ulcer.
back:
Histological zones (top to bottom):
- Necrotic fibrinoid debris.
- Zone of active neutrophilic inflammation.
- Vascularized granulation tissue.
- Deep collagenous/fibrotic scar.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Peptic ulcers are most frequently found in the [___] duodenum, typically within a few centimeters of the pyloric valve.
back:
Proximal. Key points:
- Usually solitary, sharply punched-out defects.
- Associated with H. pylori-induced antral gastritis.
- Occur due to increased acid load entering the duodenum.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A patient with a severe burn injury develops an acute duodenal ulcer. Identify this specific lesion type and its underlying cause.
back:
Curling Ulcer. Key points:
- Occurs in the proximal duodenum.
- Pathogenesis involves systemic hypovolemia and mucosal ischemia.
- Ischemia leads to impaired mucosal defenses and cell death.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Explain how H. pylori infection confined to the gastric antrum leads to duodenal ulceration.
back:
Pathogenetic mechanism:
- Antral infection increases local gastrin production.
- Elevated gastrin stimulates parietal cell hyperplasia in the gastric body.
- Increased acid secretion overwhelms duodenal bicarbonate defenses.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Contrast the physiological mechanism of Cushing ulcers with that of Curling ulcers.
back:
Pathophysiological contrast:
- Cushing: Intracranial injury causes vagal stimulation and acid hypersecretion.
- Curling: Severe burns cause systemic hypotension and mucosal ischemia.
- Both represent acute stress-related mucosal injury.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Identify the most common life-threatening complication of peptic ulcer disease and its presentation.
back:
Gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Key points:
- Occurs in up to 20% of patients.
- Presents as hematemesis or melena.
- Caused by ulcer erosion into an underlying vessel.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: NSAIDs promote peptic ulceration primarily by inhibiting the enzyme [___], which leads to decreased synthesis of protective prostaglandins E2 and I2.
back:
• Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2).
• Result: Reduced mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
• Impaired mucosal blood flow.
• Decreased epithelial regenerative capacity.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A 45-year-old male presents with epigastric burning pain that occurs 2 hours after meals and is relieved by food. Identify the most likely location of the lesion and the primary causative organism.
back:
• Location: Proximal duodenum.
• Pathogen: Helicobacter pylori.
• Pathophysiology: Increased acid secretion and decreased duodenal bicarbonate.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Explain the role of the bacterial enzyme urease in the survival and pathogenesis of H. pylori within the gastric lumen.
back:
• Converts urea into ammonia and CO2.
• Ammonia neutralizes gastric acid, creating a protective alkaline 'cloud'.
• Facilitates bacterial survival and colonization in the acidic environment.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A patient presents with multiple shallow gastric ulcers after a severe head injury. Contrast the mechanism of these lesions with those following extensive thermal burns.
back:
• Cushing Ulcers (Head injury): Vagal nuclei stimulation causing gastric acid hypersecretion.
• Curling Ulcers (Burns): Systemic hypotension leading to mucosal ischemia and impaired defenses.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Describe the physiological role of Prostaglandins E2 and I2 in maintaining the gastric mucosal barrier.
back:
• Stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
• Enhance mucosal blood flow via vasodilation.
• Promote epithelial restitution and suppress acid production.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: The microscopic base of a chronic peptic ulcer is classically composed of four layers; the deepest layer, which distinguishes it from an acute erosion, is [___].
back:
• Fibrous/Collagenous Scar.
• Layer 1: Necrotic debris.
• Layer 2: Non-specific acute inflammation (neutrophils).
• Layer 3: Granulation tissue.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A 60-year-old female on long-term aspirin therapy presents with sudden onset severe abdominal pain and 'free air under the diaphragm' on X-ray. Identify the complication and the most likely ulcer site.
back:
• Complication: Perforation causing peritonitis.
• Site: Anterior wall of the duodenum or stomach.
• Surgical emergency due to leakage of gastric contents.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Describe the morphologic features that distinguish a benign peptic ulcer from a malignant gastric carcinoma on gross inspection.
back:
• Benign: Small (<3cm), punched-out, smooth level margins, clean base.
• Malignant: Large, irregular everted/heaped-up margins, necrotic or hemorrhagic base.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Contrast the acid secretion profiles and H. pylori distribution between antral-predominant gastritis and pangastritis.
back:
• Antral-predominant: Increased acid; high risk of duodenal ulcers.
• Pangastritis: Decreased acid (atrophy); associated with gastric adenocarcinoma risk and intestinal metaplasia.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Identify the most common site for the development of a peptic ulcer in the stomach.
back:
• Lesser curvature.
• Location: Usually at the interface of the body and antrum.
• Frequently solitary (80% of cases).

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: The spiral-shaped, Gram-negative organism responsible for the majority of cases of chronic antral gastritis and subsequent peptic ulceration is [___].
back:
Helicobacter pylori
- Gram-negative spiral bacillus.
- Most common cause of PUD.
- Produces urease to survive gastric pH.
- Linked to MALToma and adenocarcinoma.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: A 45-year-old male presents with epigastric burning that is relieved by eating but recurs 2-3 hours later and frequently wakes him at night. Identify the most likely anatomical site of the lesion.
back:
Duodenum (Proximal)
- Characterized by the 'pain-food-relief' cycle.
- Pain typically occurs 1-3 hours after meals.
- Associated with increased gastric acid secretion.
- Most common site for chronic PUD.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Explain the primary mechanism by which non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) disrupt the gastric mucosal barrier to induce ulceration.
back:
COX-1/COX-2 Inhibition:
- Depletes protective prostaglandins (E2, I2).
- Reduces mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
- Decreases mucosal blood flow and restitution.
- Impairs acid suppression and epithelial defense.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Contrast the gross morphological margins of a benign peptic ulcer with those typically found in a malignant gastric carcinoma.
back:
Benign vs. Malignant Gross Features:
- Benign: Solitary, punched-out, smooth clean base, straight margins.
- Malignant: Irregular, heaped-up, necrotic base, larger size.
- Benign mucosal folds radiate from the center.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
front: Identify the specific physiological mechanism behind the development of 'Cushing ulcers' in patients with severe intracranial disease.
back:
Vagal Nuclei Hyperactivation:
- Intracranial lesions stimulate vagal nuclei.
- Leads to excessive gastric acid secretion.
