• Results in profuse watery, non-bloody diarrhea
• Usually lacks significant mucosal inflammation.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: A 5-year-old presents with bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked ground beef. Lab findings show hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes. Identify the most likely pathogen and the associated complication.
back:
• Pathogen: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC/E. coli O157:H7)
• Complication: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
• Pathogenesis: Shiga toxin enters the bloodstream causing systemic endothelial damage.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Explain the role of bacterial toxins in the development of Pseudomembranous colitis following broad-spectrum antibiotic use.
back:
• Agent: Clostridium difficile
• Mechanism: Production of Cytotoxins (Toxin A and B)
• Result: Mucosal necrosis and inflammation
• Morphology: Formation of characteristic yellowish-white mucosal plaques (pseudomembranes).

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
coreConcept: Food Poisoning vs. Intestinal Infection Timing
front: Contrast the clinical onset timing and source between diarrhea caused by preformed exotoxins versus that caused by bacterial colonization.
back:
• Preformed Toxins (S. aureus, B. cereus): Rapid onset within 6 hours of ingestion.
• Colonization/Infection (Salmonella, ETEC): Delayed onset, typically >12-24 hours.
• S. aureus is linked to dairy/meats; B. cereus is linked to reheated rice.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Identify the specific pharmacological reason why Ciprofloxacin is generally avoided in children suspected of having Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) infection.
back:
• Increases Shiga toxin release from bacteria
• Significantly elevates the risk of developing Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
• Management focuses on supportive care and hydration.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: In an immunocompromised patient with chronic watery diarrhea, the presence of oocysts on an [___] stain of the stool is diagnostic for Cryptosporidium hominis.
back:
• Acid-fast stain
• Cryptosporidium is a major cause of diarrhea in AIDS patients
• Can cause large outbreaks via contaminated water supplies.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: A hiker presents with persistent foul-smelling, fatty stools and abdominal bloating after drinking stream water. Stool analysis reveals pear-shaped trophozoites with two nuclei. State the diagnosis and the typical treatment.
back:
• Diagnosis: Giardiasis (Giardia lamblia)
• Treatment: Metronidazole or Tinidazole
• Key feature: Malabsorptive diarrhea that can persist for weeks.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Explain the pathophysiological link between a Campylobacter jejuni infection and the subsequent development of ascending muscle weakness.
back:
• Mechanism: Molecular mimicry between bacterial antigens and nerve gangliosides
• Condition: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)
• Result: Immune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Distinguish between the stool microscopy findings of Shigella dysentery and Rotavirus gastroenteritis.
back:
• Shigella: Presence of blood, pus (neutrophils), and mucus (inflammatory).
• Rotavirus: Watery stool lacking blood, pus, or significant leukocytes (non-inflammatory).
• Shigella involves mucosal invasion; Rotavirus involves osmotic/secretory disruption.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Identify the Gram-negative rod that causes mesenteric adenitis, often presenting with fever and right lower quadrant pain mimicking acute appendicitis.
back:
• Yersinia enterocolitica
• Transmitted via contaminated food/water
• Diagnosed via stool culture on special media.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: The bacterial pathogen most frequently implicated in the etiology of 'traveler's diarrhea' through the production of heat-labile and heat-stable enterotoxins is [___].
back:
• Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC)
• Causes secretory, non-inflammatory watery diarrhea
• Primarily affects the small intestine
• Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: An outbreak of nausea, projectile vomiting, and watery diarrhea occurs in a nursing home facility. The most likely viral agent responsible for this self-limited presentation is [___].
back:
• Norovirus
• Leading cause of gastroenteritis outbreaks in closed environments
• Characterized by a very low infectious dose
• Clinical diagnosis based on rapid spread and short duration

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism of Vibrio cholerae enterotoxin leading to massive secretory diarrhea.
back:
• Activates the Gs alpha subunit of G-proteins
• Causes permanent activation of adenylate cyclase
• Increases intracellular cAMP levels
• Triggers massive chloride secretion and inhibits sodium absorption

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Contrast the diagnostic findings of non-inflammatory (watery) diarrhea with inflammatory (bloody) diarrhea.
back:
• Non-inflammatory: Absent fecal leukocytes; involves small bowel; primarily secretory/osmotic
• Inflammatory: Fecal leukocytes and blood present; involves colon; involves mucosal invasion or cytotoxin-mediated damage

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Outline the pharmacological management steps for mild versus severe pseudomembranous colitis caused by Clostridium difficile.
back:
• Mild-to-moderate: Oral Metronidazole
• Severe: Oral Vancomycin
• Supportive: Discontinuation of the inciting antibiotic
• Recurrent: Consider Fidaxomicin or fecal microbiota transplant

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: The major viral cause of severe, dehydrating diarrhea in infants and young children, often presenting with a fever and vomiting prodrome, is [___].
back:
• Rotavirus
• Primary cause of childhood diarrheal mortality globally
• Destroys mature enterocytes in the small intestine
• Vaccine-preventable; diagnosis via stool PCR

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: A hiker presents with foul-smelling, fatty stools (steatorrhea) and abdominal bloating after drinking untreated stream water. Identify the pathogen and its classic diagnostic stage.
back:
• Giardia lamblia
• Pear-shaped trophozoites or oval cysts seen in stool
• Trophozoites attach to the intestinal brush border via a ventral sucking disk

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Describe the systemic progression and laboratory findings when Shiga toxin from STEC enters the circulation.
back:
• Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
• Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (Schistocytes on smear)
• Thrombocytopenia (platelet consumption)
• Acute Kidney Injury (endothelial damage to glomerular capillaries)

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Distinguish between the food poisoning caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Salmonella regarding incubation period.
back:
• S. aureus: Short (1-6 hours); caused by preformed enterotoxins
• Salmonella: Longer (12-72 hours); requires bacterial multiplication and mucosal invasion
• S. aureus focuses on vomiting; Salmonella includes fever/inflammatory diarrhea

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: List the three most common bacterial pathogens responsible for causing bacillary dysentery (bloody diarrhea with pus).
back:
• Shigella species (most common)
• Campylobacter jejuni
• Non-typhoidal Salmonella
• Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) also presents similarly

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Helicobacter pylori utilizes specific surface proteins known as [___] to facilitate firm attachment to surface foveolar cells, preventing bacterial washout during peristalsis.
back: Adhesins (e.g., BabA).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 55-year-old male with cirrhosis presents with occult GI bleeding. Endoscopy reveals longitudinal stripes of edematous, erythematous mucosa in the antrum (watermelon stomach). Identify the likely diagnosis.
back: Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain the sequence of events by which Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) leads to the development of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS).
back:
• Shiga toxin enters the systemic circulation.
• Toxin induces endothelial damage in glomerular capillaries.
• Microvascular thrombosis follows, causing schistocyte formation and renal failure.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the primary histological driver and gastric acid status between Ménétrier disease and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
back:
• Ménétrier: TGF-α overexpression; foveolar hyperplasia; decreased acid (achlorhydria).
• Zollinger-Ellison: Gastrin hypersecretion; parietal cell hyperplasia; massive acid hypersecretion.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Specify the most common bacterial pathogen responsible for inflammatory diarrhea and yellowish pseudomembrane formation following broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy.
back: Clostridium difficile (C. diff).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The most common bacterial cause of acute diarrhea that is strongly associated with the subsequent development of the neurological complication known as [___] is Campylobacter jejuni.
back: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A patient presents with bloody diarrhea and right upper quadrant pain. Stool microscopy reveals trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis). Identify the pathogen.
back: Entamoeba histolytica.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Describe the cellular mechanism by which CD4+ T cells induce mucosal atrophy in the gastric body during autoimmune gastritis.
back:
• T cells target H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) on parietal cells.
• Direct destruction leads to loss of acid and intrinsic factor.
• Chief cells are lost secondary to overall gland destruction.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish the typical incubation period and food source for Staphylococcus aureus versus Bacillus cereus (emetic type) food poisoning.
back:
• Both: Rapid onset (<6 hours).
• S. aureus: Meats, dairy, or mayonnaise.
• B. cereus: Reheated rice.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the characteristic anatomical location and vessel type associated with a Dieulafoy lesion.
back: Lesser curvature of the stomach, near the gastroesophageal junction; involves an abnormally large submucosal arteriole.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: H. pylori utilizes [___] to navigate through the viscous gastric mucus layer to reach the surface foveolar cells.
back:
• Flagella
• Provides essential motility in the thick mucus environment.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 5-year-old child presents with bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked ground beef, followed by oliguria and schistocytes on blood smear. The most likely pathogen is [___].
back:
• Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC / O157:H7)
• Pathogenesis: Shiga toxin enters the bloodstream causing endothelial damage and Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) induces profuse watery diarrhea.
back:
• Production of Heat-labile (LT) and Heat-stable (ST) enterotoxins.
• Toxins disrupt intestinal ion transporters.
• Results in massive secretion of chloride and water into the lumen.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the typical food sources and timing of emesis for Staphylococcus aureus versus the 'emetic form' of Bacillus cereus.
back:
• S. aureus: Dairy, mayonnaise, or meats.
• B. cereus: Reheated rice.
• Both: Symptoms occur within 6 hours due to preformed toxins.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the neurological complication classically associated with a preceding Campylobacter jejuni infection.
back:
• Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)
• Mechanism: Molecular mimicry between bacterial lipooligosaccharides and peripheral nerve gangliosides.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: In a patient with post-antibiotic diarrhea, the characteristic endoscopic finding of yellowish-white plaques on the colonic mucosa is termed [___].
back:
• Pseudomembranous colitis
• Caused by Clostridium difficile toxins (Toxin A and B).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A teenager presents with fever and right lower quadrant pain. Surgery reveals a normal appendix but enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes (mesenteric adenitis). Identify the most likely bacterial pathogen.
back:
• Yersinia enterocolitica
• Often presents as 'pseudoappendicitis'.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Describe how the H. pylori virulence factor CagA (cytotoxin-associated gene A) specifically increases the risk of gastric malignancy.
back:
• Induces proinflammatory cytokine secretion (e.g., IL-8).
• Promotes gastric atrophy and intestinal metaplasia.
• Found in 90% of isolates in high-risk cancer populations.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish the stool characteristics of Giardia lamblia infection from Entamoeba histolytica.
back:
• Giardia: Fatty, foul-smelling, non-bloody stools (steatorrhea).
• E. histolytica: Bloody diarrhea (dysentery) with mucus.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Name the non-invasive test for H. pylori that relies on the detection of labeled carbon isotopes in exhaled CO2 following ingestion of a substrate.
back:
• Urea Breath Test
• Based on bacterial urease converting urea into ammonia and labeled CO2.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: The ingestion of reheated rice contaminated with the pre-formed, heat-stable enterotoxins of [___] typically results in vomiting and diarrhea within 6 hours.
back:
• Bacillus cereus
• Symptoms are usually self-limiting within 24 hours
• Pathogenesis involves toxin-mediated disruption of intestinal absorption.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: A hiker presents with flatulence, bloating, and foul-smelling, fatty stools that float after consuming untreated wilderness water. Identify the most likely protozoan pathogen.
back:
• Giardia lamblia
• Transmitted via cysts in contaminated water
• Diagnosis via stool microscopy (trophozoites/cysts) or antigen tests.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Explain the role of Shiga toxin in the development of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) following a bacterial diarrheal illness.
back:
• Toxin enters systemic circulation from the gut
• Causes endothelial damage leading to microthrombi
• Results in triad of hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal failure.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Contrast the typical clinical mimicry of Yersinia enterocolitica with that of acute appendicitis.
back:
• Yersinia causes mesenteric adenitis and terminal ileitis
• Presents with RLQ pain and fever, simulating appendicitis
• Confirmed by stool culture on special selective media.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Identify the specific endoscopic hallmark of Clostridium difficile infection and the primary pharmacological trigger.
back:
• Finding: Yellowish mucosal plaques (pseudomembranes)
• Trigger: Recent broad-spectrum antimicrobial use
• Treatment: Oral vancomycin or metronidazole.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: The Gram-negative, curved rod [___] is the most common bacterial cause of diarrhea in many regions and is strongly associated with the post-infectious development of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
back:
• Campylobacter jejuni
• Acquired through undercooked poultry or unpasteurized milk
• Causes inflammatory (bloody) diarrhea.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Following a communal meal with mayonnaise-based salads, several individuals develop severe vomiting within 4 hours. Which mechanism best explains this rapid onset?
back:
• Ingestion of pre-formed Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin
• Very short incubation (<6 hours) because bacteria do not need to colonize
• Primarily presents as non-inflammatory watery diarrhea.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Describe the diagnostic steps for a patient suspected of having intestinal Entamoeba histolytica with possible extraintestinal involvement.
back:
• Stool O&P for cysts/trophozoites and serology
• Imaging for potential hepatic abscesses
• Treatment requires tissue agents (metronidazole) and luminal agents (paromomycin).

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Distinguish between Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) regarding their clinical stool characteristics.
back:
• ETEC: Watery, non-bloody diarrhea (Traveler's diarrhea)
• STEC: Often begins watery but progresses to bloody diarrhea (Dysentery)
• ETEC is usually afebrile.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: List the most common viral pathogen responsible for childhood diarrhea and its typical clinical prodrome.
back:
• Rotavirus
• Prodrome: Fever and vomiting followed by profuse watery diarrhea
• Leading cause of severe dehydration in infants globally.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The specific virulence factor that allows Helicobacter pylori to remain motile within the highly viscous environment of the gastric mucus is the [___].
back:
• Flagella
• Enables chemotaxis toward the neutral pH of the epithelial surface
• Critical for successful colonization of the antrum.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 70-year-old patient on broad-spectrum antibiotics for pneumonia develops profuse watery diarrhea and fever. Endoscopy reveals yellow-white adherent mucosal plaques. What is the most likely pathogen?
back:
• Clostridium difficile
• Pathogenesis: Toxin production (Toxin A and B)
• Clinical: Pseudomembranous colitis following antibiotic disruption of normal flora.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain the role of preformed toxins in the rapid clinical onset of Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning.
back:
• Symptoms begin within 1-6 hours
• Ingestion of heat-stable enterotoxin already present in food (e.g., dairy, mayonnaise)
• No bacterial colonization required for initial symptoms.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the classic clinical associations of Campylobacter jejuni with those of Yersinia enterocolitica.
back:
• C. jejuni: Associated with Guillain-Barré syndrome (molecular mimicry)
• Y. enterocolitica: Causes mesenteric adenitis that mimics acute appendicitis (pseudoappendicitis).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Briefly describe the intracellular mechanism of action of the Vibrio cholerae enterotoxin.
back:
• ADP-ribosylation of Gs protein
• Constitutive activation of Adenylate Cyclase
• Massive increase in cAMP levels
• Secretion of Cl- and water leading to 'rice-water' stools.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A traveler returning from a mountain hiking trip presents with abdominal bloating and foul-smelling, fatty stools. Diagnosis is confirmed by finding [___] in the stool samples.
back:
• Giardia lamblia (Cysts or Trophozoites)
• Pathogenesis: Adherence to brush border via ventral sucking disk
• Clinical: Malabsorptive diarrhea (steatorrhea).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 5-year-old child develops bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked beef, followed by oliguria, anemia, and schistocytes on blood smear. Name the underlying pathogenesis.
back:
• Shiga Toxin (produced by STEC/E. coli O157:H7)
• Toxin enters bloodstream, causing endothelial damage in renal capillaries
• Leads to Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain how overproduction of Transforming Growth Factor-alpha (TGF-α) leads to the clinical features of Ménétrier disease.
back:
• TGF-α hyperactivates EGFR (Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor)
• Results in massive foveolar cell hyperplasia (giant rugae)
• Causes protein-losing gastropathy and hypoproteinemia.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish between the primary settings and patient populations for Rotavirus versus Norovirus outbreaks.
back:
• Rotavirus: Leading cause of severe diarrhea in infants and young children worldwide
• Norovirus: Most common cause of outbreaks in adults, cruise ships, and nursing homes.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the endoscopic appearance and a common clinical sequela of Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE).
back:
• Appearance: Longitudinal erythematous stripes ('Watermelon stomach')
• Histology: Ectatic capillaries with fibrin thrombi
• Sequela: Chronic GI blood loss and iron deficiency anemia.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The bacterial virulence factor [___] facilitates H. pylori survival by allowing it to migrate through the highly viscous gastric mucus layer to reach the epithelial surface.
back:
• Flagella
• Provides motility in thick mucus
• Allows colonization of the neutral pH niche near foveolar cells.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Within 2 to 6 hours of eating fried rice at a restaurant, a patient develops severe nausea and projectile vomiting. Identify the likely pathogen and its pathogenesis.
back:
• Bacillus cereus
• Ingestion of preformed heat-stable emetic exotoxins
• Rapid onset indicates toxin-mediated rather than infectious process.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain the role of Clostridium difficile cytotoxins in the formation of the characteristic 'yellowish plaques' seen during colonoscopy.
back:
• Toxins cause focal mucosal necrosis
• Results in an inflammatory exudate of fibrin, mucus, and neutrophils
• This coalesces to form the diagnostic pseudomembrane.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A child develops bloody diarrhea and oliguria after eating undercooked beef. Peripheral blood smear reveals [___], which are fragmented red blood cells characteristic of the associated complication.
back:
• Schistocytes
• Indicates Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
• Caused by Shiga toxin entering the systemic circulation.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: How do CagA-positive strains of H. pylori differ from CagA-negative strains in terms of clinical progression and risk?
back:
• Induce higher proinflammatory cytokine levels
• Stronger association with gastric atrophy and intestinal metaplasia
• Significantly higher risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: In patients with suspected parasitic gastroenteritis, the presence of [___] in the stool—described as fatty, foul-smelling, and floating—is highly suggestive of Giardia lamblia infection.
back:
• Steatorrhea
• Caused by trophozoites adhering to the brush border
• Results in malabsorption and lack of intestinal invasion.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A patient presents with fever and right lower quadrant pain mimicking acute appendicitis, but imaging reveals mesenteric adenitis. Which pathogen is the most likely cause?
back:
• Yersinia enterocolitica
• Causes ileitis and mesenteric lymph node inflammation
• Transmitted via contaminated food or milk.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the primary trigger for gastric mucosal injury in a patient with systemic shock versus a patient with a severe traumatic brain injury.
back:
• Shock: Local mucosal ischemia due to splanchnic vasoconstriction/Endothelin-1
• Brain Injury: Gastric acid hypersecretion via direct vagal nuclei stimulation.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish the microscopic distribution of inflammatory infiltrates in H. pylori-associated gastritis from those seen in autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
back:
• H. pylori: Superficial lamina propria inflammation (neutrophils and plasma cells)
• Autoimmune: Deep, diffuse lymphocytic/macrophage infiltrate centered on gastric glands.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the specific histological feature induced by chronic H. pylori infection that provides a substrate for the development of MALT lymphoma.
back:
• Induced lymphoid aggregates
• Often contain germinal centers
• Represent acquired mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
coreConcept: ETEC as Primary Agent of Traveler's Diarrhea
front: The most common bacterial cause of 'traveler's diarrhea,' characterized by watery, non-bloody stools without fever, is [___].
back: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC).

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: A 4-year-old presents with bloody diarrhea after consuming an undercooked burger. He subsequently develops oliguria and anemia with schistocytes. Identify the pathogen and the resulting complication.
back:
• Pathogen: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC/O157:H7).
• Complication: Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS).
• HUS triad: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which Vibrio cholerae and ETEC toxins induce profuse watery diarrhea.
back:
• Secretion of enterotoxins (e.g., Cholera toxin).
• Toxins increase intracellular cAMP or cGMP.
• Stimulates active chloride secretion and inhibits sodium absorption.
• Leads to massive osmotic movement of water into the lumen.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Contrast the typical clinical settings and target populations for Norovirus versus Rotavirus outbreaks.
back:
• Norovirus: Affects all ages; associated with cruise ships, schools, and nursing homes.
• Rotavirus: Primarily infants and young children; presents with a fever/vomiting prodrome before diarrhea.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Identify the protozoan agent associated with fatty, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea) and flatulence in hikers consuming untreated water.
back:
• Giardia lamblia (or Giardia duodenalis).
• Diagnosis: Trophozoites or cysts in stool; stool antigen test.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: The development of yellowish mucosal plaques (pseudomembranes) following broad-spectrum antibiotic use is pathognomonic for infection by [___].
back: Clostridium difficile.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: A patient develops intense vomiting and abdominal cramps exactly 4 hours after eating reheated fried rice. Identify the most likely pathogen and its virulence factor.
back:
• Pathogen: Bacillus cereus.
• Virulence: Preformed heat-stable emetic toxin.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Explain the difference in pathogenic mechanism between Shigella-induced diarrhea and ETEC-induced diarrhea.
back:
• Shigella: Directly invades intestinal mucosa and produces cytotoxins, causing inflammation and bloody stools.
• ETEC: Non-invasive; produces enterotoxins that disrupt ion transport without mucosal destruction.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Distinguish between the microscopic stool findings for Cryptosporidium hominis and Entamoeba histolytica.
back:
• Cryptosporidium: Small, acid-fast positive oocysts.
• Entamoeba histolytica: Trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis) or quadrinucleate cysts.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Name two bacterial pathogens commonly causing mesenteric adenitis that clinically mimics acute appendicitis.
back:
• Yersinia enterocolitica.
• Campylobacter jejuni.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: The primary viral pathogen responsible for large-scale outbreaks of afebrile watery diarrhea in closed environments like cruise ships and nursing homes is [___].
back:
• Norovirus
• Most common cause of viral gastroenteritis
• Spreads via fecal-oral route
• Symptoms include vomiting and abdominal cramps

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: A 5-year-old child presents with bloody diarrhea followed by oliguria and schistocytes on blood smear after eating a hamburger. Identify the specific bacterial strain and its primary virulence factor.
back:
• Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC/O157:H7)
• Virulence Factor: Shiga toxin
• Causes Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
• Pathogenesis: Capillary endothelial damage

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Explain the role of preformed exotoxins in the rapid onset of symptoms associated with certain foodborne illnesses.
back:
• Symptoms occur within 6 hours of ingestion
• No bacterial colonization required for initial illness
• Common agents: S. aureus and B. cereus
• Typically presents as severe vomiting

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: A hiker presents with persistent foul-smelling, fatty stools and bloating after drinking untreated stream water. Contrast the microscopic diagnostic findings for this agent with those of Entamoeba histolytica.
back:
• Giardia lamblia: Pear-shaped trophozoites with 'owl-eye' nuclei or cysts
• Entamoeba histolytica: Trophozoites with ingested red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis)
• Giardia causes malabsorption; Amoeba causes invasive dysentery

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Enumerate the characteristic endoscopic finding and the standard drug treatment for moderate antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis.
back:
• Finding: Adherent yellowish-white mucosal plaques (pseudomembranes)
• Primary agent: Clostridium difficile
• Treatment: Oral Metronidazole (mild/moderate) or Vancomycin (severe)

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: The gram-negative rod [___] is a common cause of bloody diarrhea, is frequently acquired from poultry or reptiles, and is notable for causing mesenteric adenitis that mimics appendicitis.
back:
• Salmonella species (Non-typhoidal)
• Acquired from eggs, dairy, or pet turtles
• May present with low-grade fever
• Usually self-limited in healthy hosts

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: A patient with AIDS and a very low CD4 count presents with chronic, profuse watery diarrhea. Identify the likely acid-fast positive protozoan and its environmental source.
back:
• Cryptosporidium hominis
• Source: Contaminated community water supplies
• Diagnosis: Oocysts seen on acid-fast stool stain
• Can involve biliary and respiratory tracts

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Describe the physiological impact of Shiga toxin entering the bloodstream and its association with antibiotic use in pediatric patients.
back:
• Induces systemic microvascular thrombosis
• Antibiotics (e.g., Ciprofloxacin) may increase toxin release
• Increases risk of renal failure and HUS
• Primarily affects children and elderly

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Contrast the typical age group and clinical prodrome of Rotavirus infection versus Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC).
back:
• Rotavirus: Children; fever and vomiting precede watery diarrhea
• ETEC: Travelers ('Traveler's Diarrhea'); watery diarrhea without significant fever
• ETEC uses enterotoxins (LT/ST) to increase cAMP/cGMP

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Identify the curved, gram-negative rod that is the leading cause of bacterial diarrhea and is a well-known trigger for Guillain-Barré syndrome.
back:
• Campylobacter jejuni
• Grows on special media at 42°C
• Acquired from undercooked poultry
• Pathogenesis: Mucosal invasion and inflammation

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Rapid onset of vomiting and epigastric pain within [___] hours of consuming contaminated dairy or mayonnaise is characteristic of Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning.
back:
• 6 hours.
• Mediated by preformed, heat-stable enterotoxins.
• Symptoms typically resolve within 1–2 days with supportive care.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A college student presents with acute vomiting and abdominal cramps 4 hours after eating leftover fried rice. Identify the most likely pathogen and the state of its toxin.
back:
• Bacillus cereus.
• Preformed emetic toxin produced during germination of spores.
• Common in reheated rice or starchy foods.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain how Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) toxins alter enterocyte signaling to cause watery diarrhea.
back:
• Heat-Labile toxin (LT) activates Adenylate Cyclase, increasing cAMP.
• Heat-Stable toxin (ST) activates Guanylate Cyclase, increasing cGMP.
• Both lead to chloride secretion and inhibition of sodium absorption.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the clinical risk of using fluoroquinolones in pediatric Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) versus Shigella infections.
back:
• STEC: Antibiotics increase Shiga toxin release, significantly raising the risk of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS).
• Shigella: Antibiotics (e.g., Ciprofloxacin) are indicated to shorten the disease course and reduce person-to-person shedding.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the endoscopic hallmark of Clostridium difficile infection and the specific roles of its two primary toxins.
back:
• Yellowish-white mucosal plaques (Pseudomembranes).
• Toxin A: Enterotoxin causing inflammation and fluid secretion.
• Toxin B: Cytotoxin causing direct epithelial necrosis and cytoskeletal disruption.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The presence of foul-smelling, fatty stools (steatorrhea) and bloating in a patient with a history of drinking untreated mountain stream water is diagnostic for [___].
back:
• Giardia lamblia.
• Pathogenesis involves trophozoites adhering to the brush border, causing malabsorption.
• Diagnosed via stool antigen tests or O&P (cysts/trophozoites).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A patient presents with bloody diarrhea followed by ascending paralysis and areflexia. Name the likely inciting organism and the mechanism of this neurological complication.
back:
• Campylobacter jejuni.
• Molecular mimicry between bacterial lipooligosaccharides and host gangliosides.
• Leads to Guillain-Barré Syndrome; also associated with reactive arthritis.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Describe the characteristic microscopic appearance of Entamoeba histolytica in intestinal tissue and the resulting gross ulcer morphology.
back:
• Flask-shaped ulcers with narrow necks and broad submucosal bases.
• Trophozoites frequently show erythrophagocytosis (ingested RBCs).
• Can progress to hepatic 'anchovy paste' abscesses.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish between the typical stool findings and systemic features of Non-typhoidal Salmonella versus Vibrio cholerae.
back:
• Salmonella: Inflammatory diarrhea (blood/pus), fever, and fecal leukocytes present.
• Vibrio cholerae: Non-inflammatory 'rice-water' stools, no fever, no blood, massive osmotic water loss.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: List three common non-human reservoirs of Non-typhoidal Salmonella and the specific surgical mimicry it can cause in children.
back:
• Reservoirs: Undercooked poultry/eggs, unpasteurized dairy, and pet reptiles (turtles/snakes).
• Mimicry: Can cause mesenteric adenitis, mimicking acute appendicitis (similar to Yersinia).

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: The specific bacterial agent associated with rapid-onset emesis and diarrhea after consuming reheated fried rice is [___].
back:
* Bacillus cereus.
* Mediated by preformed heat-stable emetic toxins.
* Symptoms typically occur within 1–6 hours of ingestion.
* Diagnosis is largely clinical or via food toxin analysis.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: A 25-year-old traveler returns from a rural area with profuse watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping but no fever. Identify the most likely pathogen and its primary mechanism.
back:
* Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC).
* Primary cause of 'Traveler’s Diarrhea'.
* Mediated by heat-labile (LT) and heat-stable (ST) enterotoxins.
* These toxins stimulate fluid and electrolyte secretion into the intestinal lumen.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Explain the diagnostic utility of stool testing versus endoscopy in a patient suspected of Clostridium difficile infection.
back:
* Stool analysis (PCR or Enzyme Immunoassay) detects A and B toxins.
* Colonoscopy identifies characteristic raised, yellowish-white 'pseudomembranes'.
* Histology shows focal epithelial necrosis with erupting 'volcano' fibrinopurulent exudates.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Contrast the risk of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) between Shigella and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) infections in children.
back:
* STEC (O157:H7) is the leading trigger for HUS in children.
* STEC toxin enters the bloodstream, damaging glomerular endothelial cells.
* Use of certain antibiotics (e.g., fluoroquinolones) for STEC increases HUS risk; not a primary concern with Shigella.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Identify the preferred pharmacological treatment for a patient diagnosed with moderate Pseudomembranous colitis.
back:
* Oral Metronidazole is typically used for mild-to-moderate episodes.
* Oral Vancomycin is the preferred agent for severe or recurrent cases.
* Treatment must include discontinuation of the offending antibiotic when possible.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: On special MacConkey-sorbitol culture media, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) is distinguished from other E. coli strains because it fails to ferment [___].
back:
* Sorbitol.
* Most E. coli strains are sorbitol fermenters (turn pink).
* STEC (O157:H7) appears as colorless colonies (sorbitol-negative).
* Essential for screening in patients with bloody diarrhea.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: A child presents with low-grade fever and bloody diarrhea after exposure to a pet turtle. Identify the most likely pathogen and common dietary sources.
back:
* Non-typhoidal Salmonella.
* Associated with pet reptiles (turtles, snakes).
* Dietary sources include undercooked poultry, raw eggs, and unpasteurized milk.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Explain how Yersinia enterocolitica infection can clinically mimic an acute surgical emergency.
back:
* It causes terminal ileitis and mesenteric adenitis.
* Presents with right lower quadrant (RLQ) pain and fever.
* Clinically indistinguishable from acute appendicitis in many cases.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: Distinguish the primary pathophysiological mechanisms of watery diarrhea versus inflammatory (bloody) diarrhea.
back:
* Watery: Pathogens (e.g., Vibrio cholerae) use enterotoxins to disrupt ion transport without causing cell death.
* Inflammatory: Pathogens use mucosal invasion (e.g., Shigella) or cytotoxins (e.g., C. difficile) to cause epithelial necrosis and hemorrhage.

category: Enumerate common infectious agents of diarrheal diseases
front: List the classic stool characteristics and the gold-standard diagnostic method for Giardia lamblia.
back:
* Foul-smelling, fatty, non-bloody stools (steatorrhea/malabsorption).
* Persistent abdominal bloating and flatulence.
* Diagnosis via stool microscopy for cysts/trophozoites or stool antigen (ELISA) assays.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: In Ménétrier disease, giant cerebriform rugal folds result from excessive secretion of [___], leading to foveolar hyperplasia and protein-losing enteropathy.
back: • Transforming growth factor (TGF)-alpha. • Hyperactivation of EGFR. • Causes hypoproteinemia and weight loss.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: An elderly patient with cirrhosis undergoes endoscopy, revealing longitudinal stripes of edematous, erythematous antral mucosa. Identify the condition.
back: • Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE). • Known as 'Watermelon stomach'. • Histology shows dilated capillaries with fibrin thrombi.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain how the enterotoxins of Vibrio cholerae and Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) induce massive watery diarrhea.
back: • Increase intracellular cAMP or cGMP. • Open CFTR chloride channels in crypt cells. • Lead to massive secretion of Cl- and water.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) and Shigella regarding their typical stool culture characteristics and reservoirs.
back: • STEC: Does not ferment sorbitol; Cattle reservoir. • Shigella: Ferments glucose; Human reservoir only. • STEC carries higher risk of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the vascular anomaly characterized by an abnormally large submucosal arteriole that erodes overlying epithelium near the gastroesophageal junction.
back: • Dieulafoy lesion. • Found in the lesser curvature. • Causes recurrent, copious, self-limited gastric bleeding.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The most common bacterial cause of diarrhea, [___], is uniquely associated with the post-infectious development of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
back: • Campylobacter jejuni. • Gram-negative curved rod. • Requires special culture media like Skirrow agar.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 12-year-old child presents with fever and severe right lower quadrant pain mimicking appendicitis. Stool culture grows Gram-negative rods on special medium. What is the diagnosis?
back: • Yersinia enterocolitica. • Causes mesenteric adenitis (pseudo-appendicitis). • Often acquired from contaminated milk or pork.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain why Giardia lamblia infection typically results in fatty, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea).
back: • Trophozoites attach to brush border via ventral discs. • Create physical and enzymatic barriers to fat absorption. • Leads to malabsorption and flatulence.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES) from typical Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) regarding ulcer location and gastrin levels.
back: • ZES: Multiple ulcers in unusual sites (jejunum); marked hypergastrinemia. • PUD: Usually solitary (antrum/duodenum); normal or modest gastrin rise.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the protozoan pathogen that causes chronic watery diarrhea in AIDS patients and is detected via acid-fast staining of stool.
back: • Cryptosporidium hominis. • Red-stained oocysts on acid-fast stain. • Transmitted via contaminated water; chlorine resistant.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The specific structural adaptation that enables Helicobacter pylori to remain motile within the highly viscous gastric mucus is the [___].
back:
- Flagella.
- Allows bacteria to traverse thick mucus layers.
- Facilitates successful colonization of the gastric surface epithelium.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A group of office workers develops severe vomiting and epigastric pain exactly 4 hours after consuming chicken salad at a picnic. No fever is reported. Identify the likely pathogen and the mechanism of injury.
back:
- Staphylococcus aureus.
- Caused by ingestion of preformed heat-stable enterotoxins.
- Rapid onset (typically <6 hours) differentiates it from infection-based gastroenteritis.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain how the H. pylori virulence factor CagA (cytotoxin-associated gene A) contributes to the development of gastric adenocarcinoma.
back:
- Injected via bacterial type IV secretion system.
- Stimulates host proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF).
- Promotes gastric atrophy and intestinal metaplasia.
- Present in 90% of isolates in high-cancer populations.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the primary anatomical site and the resulting gastric acid production levels between H. pylori-associated gastritis and autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
back:
- H. pylori: Primarily involves the Antrum; acid levels are normal to increased.
- Autoimmune: Primarily involves the Body/Fundus; acid levels are decreased (achlorhydria) due to parietal cell destruction.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the characteristic endoscopic finding and the primary predisposing factor for colitis caused by Clostridium difficile.
back:
- Endoscopy: Yellowish mucosal plaques (pseudomembranes).
- Predisposing Factor: Prior antimicrobial (antibiotic) use.
- Pathogenesis: Toxin-mediated mucosal damage and inflammatory exudate.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Children infected with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) are at high risk of [___], a syndrome characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.
back:
- Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS).
- Triggered by Shiga toxin entering the systemic circulation.
- Blood smear reveals schistocytes (fragmented RBCs).
- Ciprofloxacin use increases HUS risk in children.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A hiker presents with long-standing abdominal cramps, flatulence, and foul-smelling, fatty stools that float. Name the causative protozoan and its diagnostic feature in stool analysis.
back:
- Giardia lamblia.
- Diagnosis: Identification of pear-shaped trophozoites or cysts in stool O&P.
- Mechanism: Malabsorption caused by trophozoite attachment to intestinal mucosa.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Delineate the mechanism by which autoimmune atrophic gastritis leads to the development of pernicious anemia.
back:
- T-cell mediated destruction of parietal cells.
- Leads to loss of Intrinsic Factor (IF).
- IF loss prevents Vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum.
- Results in megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish between Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) and Shigella based on their clinical diarrheal presentation and primary mechanism.
back:
- ETEC: Watery, non-bloody diarrhea; non-inflammatory; mediated by enterotoxins.
- Shigella: Bloody diarrhea (dysentery); inflammatory; mediated by mucosal invasion and cytotoxins.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Name the Gram-negative rod associated with contaminated poultry and raw milk that is a major precipitant of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
back:
- Campylobacter jejuni.
- Presents with fever and bloody diarrhea.
- Triggers GBS via molecular mimicry between bacterial lipooligosaccharides and human nerve gangliosides.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The bacterial factor [___] allows H. pylori to remain motile within the highly viscous gastric mucus layer to reach the neutral-pH epithelial surface.
back: Flagella. Provides necessary motility to navigate thick mucus. Essential for colonizing the ecological niche near surface foveolar cells.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 60-year-old female with cirrhosis presents with iron deficiency anemia. Endoscopy reveals longitudinal erythematous stripes in the gastric antrum ('watermelon stomach'). Identify the pathology.
back: Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE). Characterized by dilated mucosal capillaries containing fibrin thrombi. Often associated with systemic sclerosis or cirrhosis.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain the immunological mechanism driving the destruction of parietal cells in autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
back: CD4+ T-cell Mediated Injury. T-cells target the H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump). Leads to oxyntic atrophy, achlorhydria, and secondary loss of chief cells.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) and Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) regarding stool appearance and major systemic risk.
back: STEC vs ETEC. STEC: Bloody diarrhea; high risk of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS). ETEC: Watery, non-bloody diarrhea; known as 'Traveler's diarrhea'; no HUS risk.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Characterize the pathophysiology and endoscopic appearance of Ménétrier disease.
back: Hypertrophic Gastropathy. Caused by excessive TGF-alpha secretion and EGFR activation. Endoscopy reveals giant 'cerebriform' rugal folds with protein-losing enteropathy.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Recurrent upper GI bleeding from an abnormally large, pulsating submucosal arteriole (usually near the gastroesophageal junction) is a [___].
back: Dieulafoy Lesion. Caused by an arteriole that erodes overlying epithelium. Presents as copious, intermittent hematemesis without a prior history of ulcers.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A hiker presents with 3 weeks of bloating, flatulence, and foul-smelling, fatty stools after drinking stream water. Identify the most likely pathogen and diagnostic finding.
back: Giardia lamblia. Diagnosis via stool ova and parasite (O&P) analysis for pear-shaped trophozoites or cysts. Causes malabsorption due to mucosal adherence.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: How does chronic H. pylori infection facilitate the development of Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT) lymphoma?
back: Induced Lymphoid Aggregates. Chronic inflammation induces MALT containing B-cells. Prolonged antigenic stimulation leads to monoclonal B-cell transformation into low-grade lymphoma.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish the typical sources and potential post-infectious neurologic complications of Salmonella versus Campylobacter jejuni.
back: Salmonella vs Campylobacter. Salmonella: Undercooked eggs/poultry or pet reptiles. Campylobacter: Undercooked poultry; strongly associated with Guillain-Barré Syndrome via molecular mimicry.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the primary bacterial pathogens that cause mesenteric adenitis, clinically mimicking acute appendicitis.
back: Pseudoappendicitis Pathogens. Yersinia enterocolitica (most common). Campylobacter jejuni and Salmonella. Presents with RLQ pain, fever, and leukocytosis.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The bacterial virulence factor [___] is present in nearly 90% of Helicobacter pylori isolates in populations with high gastric cancer rates and promotes proinflammatory cytokine secretion.
back:
• Cytotoxin-associated gene A (CagA)
• Induces gastric atrophy and intestinal metaplasia
• Increases risk of gastric adenocarcinoma
• Found in only 50% of H. pylori isolates globally.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 6-year-old child presents with bloody diarrhea after eating an undercooked hamburger, followed by oliguria and schistocytes on blood smear. What is the underlying pathogenesis?
back:
• Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) infection
• Toxin enters bloodstream damaging endothelial cells
• Leads to Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
• Features: Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, renal failure.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain why symptoms of Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning occur rapidly, typically within 1 to 6 hours of ingestion.
back:
• Caused by ingestion of preformed heat-stable enterotoxins
• Not dependent on bacterial colonization or growth in vivo
• Common in dairy, mayonnaise, or meat products
• Resolves within 24-48 hours.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the primary pathogenic mechanisms of Shigella versus Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) in causing diarrhea.
back:
• Shigella: Mucosal invasion and Shiga toxin production (Inflammatory/Bloody)
• ETEC: Enterotoxin production (LT/ST) without invasion (Non-inflammatory/Watery)
• Shigella involves the colon; ETEC involves the small intestine.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the specific gram-negative, comma-shaped enteric pathogen strongly associated with the subsequent development of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
back:
• Campylobacter jejuni
• Most common cause of bacterial gastroenteritis
• Pathogenesis: Molecular mimicry between bacterial lipopolysaccharides and human gangliosides
• Associated with poultry ingestion.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Steatorrhea, characterized by fatty, foul-smelling stools that may float, in a hiker who drank untreated stream water is caused by [___].
back:
• Giardia lamblia (protozoan)
• Cysts or trophozoites found in stool
• Trophozoites adhere to intestinal brush border
• Causes malabsorption rather than mucosal invasion.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A patient on clindamycin therapy develops profuse diarrhea and fever. Colonoscopy shows yellowish-white mucosal plaques. What is the diagnosis and its toxic mediator?
back:
• Pseudomembranous colitis (C. difficile)
• Mediated by Toxins A (enterotoxin) and B (cytotoxin)
• Pathogenesis: Disruption of cytoskeleton/cell junctions
• Treatment: Oral Vancomycin or Metronidazole.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Describe the cellular mechanism by which Vibrio cholerae toxin leads to massive electrolyte and water loss in the small intestine.
back:
• Toxin permanently activates Gs-alpha protein
• Constitutive activation of adenylate cyclase
• Increased cAMP levels
• Opens CFTR channels leading to chloride and water secretion.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish between Salmonella and Shigella based on their natural reservoirs and infectious dose.
back:
• Salmonella: Animal reservoirs (poultry, eggs, reptiles); high infectious dose required
• Shigella: Humans are only reservoir; very low infectious dose (10-100 organisms)
• Both cause inflammatory/bloody diarrhea.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Name the pathogen responsible for causing mesenteric adenitis that frequently mimics the clinical presentation of acute appendicitis.
back:
• Yersinia enterocolitica
• Gram-negative rod; grows at cold temperatures
• Common in children
• Presents with fever, diarrhea, and right lower quadrant pain.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The diagnosis of pseudomembranous colitis is confirmed endoscopically by the presence of [___] on the colonic mucosa.
back:
• Yellowish-green plaques (pseudomembranes)
• Composed of fibrin, inflammatory cells, and necrotic debris
• Associated with Clostridium difficile toxin production.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A group of office workers develops severe nausea and vomiting exactly 4 hours after consuming a potato salad containing mayonnaise. They remain afebrile. Identify the likely pathogen and mechanism.
back:
• Staphylococcus aureus
• Ingestion of preformed heat-stable enterotoxins
• Rapid onset (typically <6 hours) and short duration.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) produces profuse watery diarrhea.
back:
• Produces Heat-labile (LT) and Heat-stable (ST) toxins
• LT increases cAMP; ST increases cGMP
• Leads to hypersecretion of chloride/water and inhibition of sodium absorption.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the typical stool characteristics and microscopic findings of Giardia lamblia versus Entamoeba histolytica.
back:
• Giardia: Non-bloody, foul-smelling, fatty stools (steatorrhea); pear-shaped trophozoites
• E. histolytica: Bloody diarrhea (dysentery); trophozoites with ingested RBCs (erythrophagocytosis).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Why is the administration of antibiotics like ciprofloxacin often avoided in children presenting with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) diarrhea?
back:
• Antibiotics may increase the release of Shiga toxin
• Significantly elevates the risk of developing Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
• HUS triad: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A common bacterial cause of inflammatory diarrhea that is uniquely associated with the development of Guillain-Barré syndrome is [___].
back:
• Campylobacter jejuni
• Most common cause of community-acquired bacterial enteritis
• Pathogenesis involves molecular mimicry between bacterial LPS and host nerve gangliosides.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 5-year-old child presents with low-grade fever and bloody diarrhea. The family recently acquired a pet turtle. Identify the pathogen and its typical transmission route.
back:
• Salmonella (non-typhoidal)
• Fecal-oral route via contaminated food (eggs, poultry) or contact with reptiles/amphibians
• Pathogenesis: Mucosal invasion and neutrophilic response.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain the pathogenesis of Bacillus cereus-associated food poisoning specifically linked to reheated rice.
back:
• Spores survive initial boiling/cooking
• Germinate and produce emetic toxin (cereulide) during slow cooling or room-temp storage
• Reheating may not inactivate the heat-stable emetic toxin.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish between 'Watery' and 'Bloody' diarrhea based on the primary site of gastrointestinal involvement and typical mechanism.
back:
• Watery: Small intestine; toxin-mediated (non-invasive); minimal inflammation
• Bloody: Colon (large intestine); mucosal invasion or cytotoxins; significant inflammation (neutrophils/pus).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the bacterial pathogen often responsible for mesenteric adenitis that clinically mimics acute appendicitis.
back:
• Yersinia enterocolitica
• Causes terminal ileitis and lymphadenitis
• Presents with right lower quadrant pain, fever, and diarrhea.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The virulence factor of H. pylori that allows the bacterium to be motile within the viscous gastric mucus layer is [___].
back:
*   Flagella
*   Enables movement towards the neutral pH of the foveolar surface

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A group of people develop severe vomiting and epigastric pain within 4 hours of eating egg salad at a picnic. Identify the likely pathogen and its specific mechanism of injury.
back:
*   Pathogen: Staphylococcus aureus
*   Mechanism: Ingestion of preformed enterotoxins (heat-stable)
*   Rapid onset (usually <6 hours)

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain how antibiotic therapy disrupts the colonic environment to facilitate Clostridium difficile-associated pseudomembranous colitis.
back:
*   Disruption of normal gut microbiota
*   C. difficile overgrowth and toxin production (Toxins A and B)
*   Formation of characteristic yellowish mucosal plaques

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 4-year-old child presents with bloody diarrhea and acute renal failure after eating undercooked beef. Contrast the likely pathogen’s mechanism with that of Vibrio cholerae.
back:
*   STEC (e.g., O157:H7): Shiga toxin causes endothelial damage and HUS
*   Vibrio cholerae: Enterotoxin increases cAMP, causing massive watery secretion without mucosal invasion

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Describe the clinical presentation of Yersinia enterocolitica that frequently leads to a surgical misdiagnosis of acute appendicitis.
back:
*   Fever and abdominal pain
*   Mesenteric adenitis
*   Acute ileitis mimicking appendiceal inflammation

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The gastrointestinal pathogen Campylobacter jejuni is uniquely associated with the post-infectious neurological complication known as [___].
back:
*   Guillain-Barre syndrome
*   Mediated by molecular mimicry between bacterial lipopolysaccharides and peripheral nerve gangliosides

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A traveler presents with chronic, foul-smelling, fatty stools and flatulence after drinking untreated water. What is the likely infectious agent and its diagnostic stage in stool?
back:
*   Agent: Giardia lamblia (protozoa)
*   Diagnosis: Detection of cysts or trophozoites in stool
*   May cause chronic malabsorption

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain the pathogenetic significance of the CagA gene in certain strains of Helicobacter pylori regarding gastric malignancy.
back:
*   Encodes cytotoxin-associated gene A
*   Induces proinflammatory cytokines (IL-8)
*   Promotes gastric atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and adenocarcinoma

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish the typical clinical timing and stool characteristics of Bacillus cereus (emetic type) from Rotavirus gastroenteritis.
back:
*   B. cereus: Symptoms begin within 6 hours; primarily vomiting; associated with reheated rice
*   Rotavirus: Longer incubation; fever followed by vomiting and watery diarrhea; common in children

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the extraintestinal organ most frequently involved in invasive Entamoeba histolytica infection and the typical nature of the lesion.
back:
*   Organ: Liver
*   Lesion: Hepatic abscess (classic 'anchovy paste' contents)
*   Symptoms: Fever, RUQ pain, and bloody diarrhea

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: The H. pylori virulence factor [___] is a spiral-shaped flagellar protein essential for movement through the viscous gastric mucus layer.
back:
• Flagella.
• Enables motility in thick mucus.
• Allows bacteria to reach the neutral pH environment of surface foveolar cells.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 22-year-old presents with bloody diarrhea and fever after eating undercooked poultry. Two weeks later, he develops ascending paralysis. Identify the likely pathogen.
back:
• Campylobacter jejuni.
• Common cause of inflammatory diarrhea.
• Associated with Guillain-Barré Syndrome via molecular mimicry.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain the cellular mechanism responsible for the destruction of parietal cells in autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
back:
• CD4+ T-cell mediated destruction.
• Targets H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) and intrinsic factor.
• Leads to achlorhydria and secondary G-cell hyperplasia.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 25-year-old nurse develops severe vomiting only 4 hours after eating a salad with mayonnaise at a picnic. Contrast this with the emetic form of Bacillus cereus.
back:
• Pathogen: Staphylococcus aureus.
• S. aureus: Source is dairy/meats/mayonnaise.
• B. cereus: Classically from reheated fried rice.
• Both: Mediated by preformed, heat-stable exotoxins.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Describe the clinical triad of Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS) following a Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) infection.
back:
• Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes).
• Thrombocytopenia.
• Acute renal failure.
• Triggered by systemic absorption of Shiga toxin.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Endoscopic visualization of discrete, yellowish-white fibrinopurulent plaques on the colonic mucosa is diagnostic of [___].
back:
• Pseudomembranous colitis.
• Pathogen: Clostridium difficile.
• Caused by Toxin A (enterotoxin) and Toxin B (cytotoxin).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A hiker presents with foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea (steatorrhea) and bloating after drinking stream water. Name the likely pathogen and its diagnostic stage in stool.
back:
• Giardia lamblia.
• Diagnostic stage: Cysts or pear-shaped trophozoites.
• Pathogenesis: Trophozoites adhere to brush border, causing malabsorption.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Detail the shared intracellular mechanism of Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) Heat-Labile (LT) toxin and Vibrio cholerae toxin.
back:
• ADP-ribosylation of Gs-alpha subunit.
• Permanent activation of adenylate cyclase.
• Increased cAMP causes massive Cl- and water secretion.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish between Salmonella and Shigella based on their primary reservoirs and infectious dose.
back:
• Salmonella: Animal reservoirs (poultry, eggs); high infectious dose.
• Shigella: Human-only reservoir; very low infectious dose (highly contagious).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the characteristic intestinal ulcer shape and the most common extraintestinal site of infection for Entamoeba histolytica.
back:
• Intestinal: Flask-shaped ulcers.
• Extraintestinal: Liver (causing 'anchovy paste' abscesses).
• Presents as bloody diarrhea (amoebic dysentery).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: In children with bloody diarrhea from STEC, the presence of distorted red blood cells called [___] on a peripheral blood smear suggests the development of Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome.
back: • Schistocytes. • Signify microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. • Result from Shiga toxin-induced microvascular thrombosis.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 70-year-old patient develops profuse bloody diarrhea and fever 10 days after finishing clindamycin. Colonoscopy reveals yellowish-white plaques on the colonic mucosa. What is the diagnosis?
back: • Pseudomembranous colitis. • Caused by Clostridium difficile toxins (A and B). • Associated with antibiotic-induced disruption of normal gut flora.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain the systemic mechanism by which Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) leads to acute renal failure.
back: • Shiga toxin enters the bloodstream. • Targets glomerular endothelial cells. • Triggers platelet activation and microthrombi formation, causing ischemic renal damage.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the typical food sources and presentation timing between Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus cereus food poisoning.
back: • S. aureus: Meats and dairy (mayonnaise); onset <6 hours. • B. cereus: Reheated fried rice; onset <6 hours. • Both involve preformed enterotoxins causing rapid vomiting.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the clinical condition caused by Yersinia enterocolitica that typically mimics acute appendicitis in pediatric patients.
back: • Mesenteric adenitis (or terminal ileitis). • Involves inflammation of mesenteric lymph nodes. • Presents with fever and right lower quadrant pain.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Stool analysis for ova and parasites in a hiker with foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea (steatorrhea) reveals characteristic pear-shaped [___] with two nuclei.
back: • Trophozoites. • Pathognomonic for Giardia lamblia. • Organism adheres to the intestinal brush border without invasion.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A patient presents with bloody diarrhea and right upper quadrant pain. Imaging reveals a hepatic 'anchovy paste' abscess. Identify the most likely protozoan pathogen.
back: • Entamoeba histolytica. • Pathogenesis involves flask-shaped mucosal ulcers. • Trophozoites can migrate via the portal vein to the liver.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: How does the virulence factor CagA (Cytotoxin-associated gene A) contribute to the development of gastric adenocarcinoma?
back: • Induces host proinflammatory cytokine release. • Promotes gastric atrophy and intestinal metaplasia. • Associated with more aggressive H. pylori strains and higher cancer risk.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the primary anatomical site of action between non-inflammatory (watery) and inflammatory (bloody) diarrhea pathogens.
back: • Watery: Primarily small intestine (disrupts fluid absorption). • Bloody: Primarily colon (causes mucosal invasion or cytotoxin-mediated destruction).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Specify the metabolic characteristic used to screen for STEC O157:H7 on MacConkey-Sorbitol (SMAC) agar.
back: • Inability to ferment sorbitol. • STEC colonies appear colorless (non-fermenters). • Distinguishes STEC from most commensal E. coli strains.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Rapid-onset vomiting and epigastric pain occurring within 6 hours of consuming reheated rice is most characteristic of the pathogen [___].
back:
• Bacillus cereus (emetic form)
• Caused by preformed heat-stable toxins
• Symptoms typically resolve within 1-2 days.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A teenager presents with fever, diarrhea, and severe right lower quadrant pain. Laparotomy reveals a normal appendix but significantly enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. Identify the likely pathogen.
back:
• Yersinia enterocolitica
• Causes mesenteric adenitis (pseudoappendicitis)
• Transmitted via contaminated food or milk.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain how Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) leads to the development of Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS).
back:
• Shiga toxin enters the bloodstream and damages endothelial cells.
• Induces microvascular thrombosis and platelet consumption.
• Results in hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the primary growth factor involved and the effect on acid secretion between Ménétrier disease and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
back:
• Ménétrier: TGF-α overexpression; results in decreased acid (foveolar hyperplasia).
• Zollinger-Ellison: Excess Gastrin; results in increased acid (parietal cell hyperplasia).

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the classic post-infectious neurological complication associated with Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis.
back:
• Guillain-Barré Syndrome
• Occurs due to molecular mimicry between bacterial lipopolysaccharides and peripheral nerve gangliosides.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A hiker presents with chronic bloating, flatulence, and foul-smelling, fatty stools that float after drinking untreated stream water. The most likely protozoan responsible is [___].
back:
• Giardia lamblia
• Interferes with fat absorption
• Diagnosed via stool ova/parasite analysis or antigen tests.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 5-year-old with a known soy protein allergy presents with epigastric pain. Biopsy of the gastric antrum shows dense eosinophilic infiltration in the mucosa and muscularis. Name the condition.
back:
• Eosinophilic gastritis
• Associated with peripheral eosinophilia and elevated IgE
• Linked to food allergens like cow's milk or soy.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Describe the specific roles of flagella and adhesins in the survival and pathogenesis of Helicobacter pylori within the gastric niche.
back:
• Flagella: Enable motility through thick, viscous gastric mucus.
• Adhesins: Facilitate firm binding to surface foveolar cells, preventing bacterial shedding into the lumen.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Distinguish between the primary mechanisms by which Vibrio cholerae and Shigella species cause diarrhea.
back:
• V. cholerae: Secretory diarrhea via enterotoxin-mediated activation of cAMP (non-invasive).
• Shigella: Inflammatory diarrhea (dysentery) via direct mucosal invasion and cytotoxin production.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Mention the specific staining technique used to identify Cryptosporidium oocysts in the stool of an immunocompromised patient.
back:
• Modified Acid-Fast stain
• Highlights oocysts as bright red/pink spheres against a blue background.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Emetic symptoms appearing within 1-6 hours of consuming reheated rice are typically caused by preformed toxins from [___].
back: • Bacillus cereus • Symptoms are caused by a heat-stable preformed enterotoxin • Characterized by rapid onset vomiting and epigastric pain • Recovery usually occurs within 24 hours.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: A 22-year-old presents with fever and bloody diarrhea. Two weeks later, he develops progressive ascending paralysis. Name the most likely pathogen.
back: • Campylobacter jejuni • Most common bacterial cause of diarrhea in many regions • Strongly associated with Guillain-Barré Syndrome via molecular mimicry • Acquired from undercooked poultry.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Explain the mechanism by which Clostridium difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis following antibiotic use.
back: • Overgrowth occurs after normal flora disruption • Produces toxins (Toxin A and B) that cause mucosal damage • Results in yellowish-white fibrinopurulent plaques (pseudomembranes) on colonoscopy • Treated with oral Vancomycin or Metronidazole.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Contrast the primary reservoirs of Salmonella (non-typhoidal) with those of Shigella.
back: • Salmonella: Animal reservoirs (poultry, eggs, pet reptiles like snakes/turtles) • Shigella: Humans are the only reservoir (transmitted person-to-person) • Salmonella causes inflammatory diarrhea; Shigella causes bacillary dysentery.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: Identify the classic clinical triad of Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS) associated with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC).
back: • Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes on smear) • Thrombocytopenia • Acute renal failure • Often follows ingestion of undercooked ground beef.

category: Discuss pathogenesis and clinical features of common pathogens
front: In patients with bloody diarrhea and fever, the presence of trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells in the stool is diagnostic for [___].
back: • Entamoeba histolytica • Can also cause flask-shaped ulcers in the colon • Frequently leads to hepatic 'anchovy paste' abscesses • Requires tissue amebicides plus luminal agents.
